Babies do not slow down because they have "run out of room" at the end of pregnancy. Do not wait until tomorrow, and do not rely on home tricks like cold drinks or sugary snacks to provoke movement. Call your maternity unit right away; monitoring is quick and painless, and the overwhelming majority of checks end in reassurance. If movements reduce again after a normal check, call again — every time counts as a fresh question. Fever and feeling unwell A high fever (commonly considered 38°C / 100.4°F or above) during pregnancy warrants a call the same day, especially with chills, pain, or feeling genuinely ill. Infections are usually simple to treat, but some need prompt attention in pregnancy. Also report burning or pain when urinating, severe vomiting or diarrhea that prevents keeping fluids down, or any illness that does not settle — dehydration and untreated infections are harder on a pregnant body. Fluid leaks and waters breaking If fluid leaks from your vagina — whether a dramatic gush or a persistent trickle that keeps dampening a pad — call your maternity unit whatever your stage of pregnancy. It may be your waters breaking, which matters both for timing labor and, before term, for getting the right care early. It can be genuinely hard to tell fluid from urine or discharge late in pregnancy; that ambiguity is precisely why teams prefer you call and let them check rather than guess at home. Preeclampsia: a cluster worth knowing Preeclampsia is a blood pressure condition of the second half of pregnancy, and its signature signs are worth memorizing as a cluster: severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling of the face, hands, or feet, pain just below the ribs (especially on the right), nausea or vomiting late in pregnancy, and sudden rapid weight gain. One reason your blood pressure and urine are checked at every prenatal visit is to catch preeclampsia before symptoms even appear. If you notice several of these signs together, call urgently — identified early, preeclampsia is closely monitored and well managed. The bottom line: better to call Save your maternity unit’s number in your phone today, along with the after-hours line. Knowing exactly who to call removes hesitation at the moment you least need it. Maternity teams universally share one message: they would far rather take a hundred calls that end in reassurance than miss the one that mattered. Calling is not overreacting — it is you doing your job. Trust your instincts; you know your body and your baby better than anyone. Report any bleeding; treat heavy bleeding or bleeding with pain as urgent. Severe headache, vision changes, or sudden face and hand swelling can signal preeclampsia — call promptly. A reduction in your baby’s movements always warrants an immediate call, every time it happens. Fever of 38°C / 100.4°F or above, painful urination, or fluid leaking all deserve same-day contact. When in doubt, call — maternity teams always prefer checking to missing something. Will I annoy my care team by calling too often? No. Answering these calls is a core part of maternity care, and teams consistently say they prefer many reassuring checks over one missed problem. If something feels off, calling is always the right move. My baby is moving less — can I wait and see? No — call your maternity unit right away rather than waiting or trying to provoke movement at home. Monitoring is quick, and most checks end in reassurance. Repeat episodes deserve repeat calls. What are the main signs of preeclampsia? Severe headache, vision changes (blurring, flashing lights), sudden swelling of the face or hands, pain below the ribs, and nausea late in pregnancy. It often develops without symptoms, which is why blood pressure is checked at every visit — but call urgently if these signs appear.

title: Creating a Birth Plan
description: How to create a birth plan that actually helps — what to include, from environment and pain relief to support people and newborn wishes, and how to stay flexible on the day.
body: A birth plan is a short, friendly document that tells your care team what matters to you during labor and birth. It is not a script the day must follow — birth famously writes its own agenda — but the process of making one helps you learn your options, and the document helps busy staff care for you as a person, not just a patient. Think of it as a conversation starter, not a contract. What a birth plan is (and is not) At its best, a birth plan is one page of clear preferences: what helps you feel safe, what you would like to try, and what matters most if decisions need to be made. It travels with your notes so anyone caring for you — including staff you have never met — can quickly understand your wishes. What it is not: a guarantee, a test you can fail, or a fixed sequence of events. The real value is in what you learn while writing it. Researching your options before labor means that if plans change on the day, you are choosing from options you already understand rather than hearing them for the first time mid-contraction. Your environment and atmosphere Think about the setting that helps you relax: dimmed lights, your own music or quiet, minimal people in the room, freedom to move around, or access to a birthing pool if available. Many units can accommodate more of this than people expect — but only if you ask. Note practical preferences too: whether you would like to use a birthing ball, shower, or bath during labor, whether you want staff to offer coaching and encouragement or keep chat minimal, and how you feel about students being present. Pain relief preferences List what you would like to try first — breathing techniques, movement and positions, water, massage, TENS — and where you stand on options like nitrous oxide and epidurals. Be honest rather than idealistic: "I would like to start without an epidural but am open to one" is a perfectly good preference. It also helps to state how you want pain relief handled in the moment: some people want staff to offer options proactively; others prefer to ask when ready and not be offered repeatedly. Either is fine — saying which saves everyone guesswork. Your support people Name who will be with you — partner, mother, friend, doula — and what roles you would like them to play, from cutting the cord to being your voice if you are deep in labor-land. If you want your birth partner present for any procedures, or want certain conversations to happen with them included, write it down. Consider a quick note about communication style: some people want everything explained as it happens; others prefer minimal narration and to be told only what is needed. Your support person can help hold that line for you. After the birth: newborn wishes The first hour after birth has its own set of choices: immediate skin-to-skin contact, delayed cord clamping, who announces the sex, who cuts the cord, and early feeding intentions — breastfeeding, formula, or wait-and-see. Note your preference on vitamin K for the baby and any cultural or religious practices that matter to your family. If a cesarean becomes part of the story, many of these wishes can still travel with you — skin-to-skin in the operating room, your playlist, your partner present. Adding a short "if a cesarean is needed" line to your plan keeps your preferences alive in every scenario. Staying flexible: plan the person, not the birth Labor is unpredictable, and the healthiest way to hold a birth plan is with a light grip. A useful exercise is to rank your top three priorities — perhaps "partner present at all times, skin-to-skin immediately, epidural available on request" — so that if events force trade-offs, everyone knows what to protect first. Some people write preferences for multiple paths: a straightforward labor, an induction, a cesarean. Far from being pessimistic, this means no version of the day can take your voice away. A changed plan is not a failed plan — the goal was always a healthy you and a healthy baby, cared for in a way that respected your wishes. Sharing it with your team Discuss your draft with your midwife or doctor around weeks 32 to 36. They will tell you what is available at your birthplace, flag anything that needs adjusting for your circumstances, and often suggest options you had not considered. This conversation is where a good plan becomes a realistic one. Keep the final version to one page, use short bullet-like lines rather than paragraphs, and bring printed copies in your hospital bag — one for your notes, one for your partner to hand over. Make sure your birth partner knows it inside out; on the day, they are its keeper. A birth plan is a one-page conversation starter about your preferences — not a contract. Cover environment, pain relief, support people, and first-hour newborn wishes. State your top three priorities so trade-offs protect what matters most. Include an "if a cesarean is needed" line so your wishes survive every scenario. Review it with your provider around weeks 32–36 and pack printed copies in your bag. Do I really need a birth plan? It is optional, but the process is valuable even if the paper never leaves your bag: writing one teaches you your options before labor, when you can think clearly, and helps your team care for you as an individual. What if my birth does not go according to the plan? Very often something changes — which is why good plans state priorities rather than scripts. A changed plan is not a failure; knowing your options in advance means you still make informed choices, whatever path the day takes. When should I write and share my birth plan? Drafting around weeks 28 to 32 and discussing it with your midwife or doctor by weeks 32 to 36 works well. That leaves time to adjust it based on their input and your birthplace’s options before labor begins.

title: What to Pack in Your Hospital Bag
description: A practical hospital bag guide — when to pack, what you, your baby, and your partner actually need, which documents to bring, and what to happily leave at home.
body: Packing the hospital bag is one of pregnancy’s most satisfying rituals — the moment the countdown becomes tangible. The trick is packing like a realist: hospitals provide more than you think, labor wards are warm, and nobody has ever needed four cute outfits on day one. Here is what genuinely earns its place in the bag. When to pack (earlier than you think) Aim to have your bag ready by around week 36 — earlier if you are expecting twins or have been told you may deliver early. Babies do not consult the calendar, and packing calmly at 35 weeks beats flinging things into a tote between contractions. Keep the bag somewhere obvious, tell your partner exactly where it lives, and leave a short list on top of any last-minute items to grab — phone chargers, toothbrushes, and the snacks you did not want going stale. If you drive, putting the bag in the car around week 38 removes one more step. For labor itself Labor is its own event with its own needs. Pack an old nightdress or oversized T-shirt you will not mourn, a lightweight robe, warm socks (feet get surprisingly cold), lip balm for all that focused breathing, and hair ties. A water bottle with a straw lets you drink in any position, and your own pillow can make an institutional room feel human. Think about your comfort toolkit too: a phone loaded with your playlist and downloaded shows, headphones, a TENS machine if you plan to use one, and massage oil or a small fan if warmth bothers you. Snacks for slow early labor — and definitely for after — are never regretted. For you, after the birth Postpartum comfort is where thoughtful packing pays off most. Bring several pairs of comfortable high-waisted underwear you will not miss (disposable ones work too), maternity pads — hospitals supply some, but you will want your own — and comfortable dark loungewear or nightwear with easy access for feeding if you plan to breastfeed. A couple of nursing bras and breast pads round out the feeding kit. Toiletries deserve real thought: your own shampoo, a toothbrush and toothpaste, a hairbrush, deodorant, and moisturizer make the first postpartum shower feel like a rebirth of its own. Add flip-flops for the shower, slippers for the ward, and a going-home outfit for yourself sized around the six-month-pregnant mark — your body has just done something enormous and deserves soft, forgiving clothes. For your baby Newborns need less than the shops suggest: a handful of sleepsuits and vests in newborn size (plus one or two in the next size up, since babies arrive in all dimensions), a hat, socks or booties, and a couple of muslin cloths for the inevitable dribbles. Pack one packet of newborn nappies and a small tub of cotton wool or sensitive wipes. For the trip home you will need a going-home outfit suited to the season, a blanket, and — non-negotiable if you are driving — a properly installed rear-facing car seat. Install and practice with it around week 36; a hospital car park is nobody’s favorite place to read instruction manuals for the first time. For your partner or support person A supported birth partner is a useful birth partner, and they need their own small kit: snacks and drinks (labor wards run long and vending machines disappoint), a phone charger — ideally an extra-long cable, since sockets are never where you want them — a change of clothes, basic toiletries, and something to pass quiet stretches. They should also carry the practical load: coins or a card for parking, the list of people to update, and knowledge of where the documents and birth plan live in the bag. If a longer stay is possible, a pillow and a light blanket for the world’s least comfortable chair-bed is partner self-care at its finest. Documents and what to leave at home Keep a folder at the top of the bag with your maternity notes or pregnancy record, photo ID, insurance or health card details as applicable where you live, your hospital paperwork, and printed copies of your birth plan. Your phone holds backups, but paper never runs out of battery. Just as important is what stays home: jewelry and valuables, large amounts of cash, your entire skincare regimen, more than one book (you will not read it), and the newborn wardrobe’s greatest hits. Hospitals are busy places with limited storage — a bag you can carry in one hand, plus a small labor day-bag, is the sweet spot. Anything forgotten can almost always be brought later by a visitor. Pack by week 36 and make sure your partner knows exactly where the bag is. For labor: an old nightdress, warm socks, lip balm, snacks, and your playlist. For after: maternity pads, comfortable underwear, dark loungewear, and your own toiletries. For baby: a few sleepsuits, a hat, nappies, and an installed rear-facing car seat for the trip home. Bring documents in one folder; leave valuables and overpacking ambitions at home. When should I have my hospital bag packed? By around week 36 for most pregnancies, and earlier if you are expecting twins or have been told you may deliver early. Keep it somewhere obvious with a short list of last-minute items to grab on top. How much should I pack for the baby? Less than instinct suggests: a few sleepsuits and vests, a hat, one packet of newborn nappies, muslins, and a season-appropriate going-home outfit. Hospitals provide the basics, and a visitor can always bring more. What documents do I need to bring? Your maternity notes or pregnancy record, photo ID, insurance or health card details as applicable, hospital paperwork, and printed copies of your birth plan — kept together in one folder at the top of the bag.

title: 4 to 8 Weeks Pregnant: Symptoms, Baby Size, First Steps
description: What to expect from 4 to 8 weeks pregnant: how your baby develops week by week, common early symptoms, your first prenatal appointment, and simple steps to take now.
body: At 8 weeks pregnant, your baby is about the size of a kidney bean, roughly 1.5 cm long, and the most common symptoms are fatigue, breast tenderness, and nausea. The weeks from 4 to 8 are some of the busiest in the whole pregnancy, even though nothing shows on the outside yet. Here is what is developing, how you might feel, and the small practical steps that matter most right now. What is developing from week 4 to week 8 At week 4, implantation is finishing. The fertilized egg has settled into the lining of your uterus, and its cells are organizing into layers that will become every organ in the body. The embryo is about the size of a poppy seed. Over weeks 5 and 6, the neural tube forms along the embryo's back. This structure becomes the brain and spinal cord, and it usually closes by around week 6, which is why folic acid matters so early. The heart is forming during these same weeks, and cardiac activity can often be seen on a transvaginal ultrasound from roughly 6 weeks, though a few days either way is common. Weeks 7 and 8 are about rapid growth and detail. Arm and leg buds appear and start to lengthen. The face begins to take shape, with early eyes, nostrils, and ears. By week 8, the embryo measures about 1.5 cm, roughly the size of a kidney bean, and it is already moving, even though you will not feel anything for months. The placenta is developing alongside all of this and will gradually take over hormone production. Because early growth follows such a predictable pace, an ultrasound measurement in these weeks gives one of the most reliable estimates of your due date. How you might feel, week by week At week 4, many people feel nothing beyond a missed period, and that is completely normal. Symptoms follow hormone levels, and hormones are only starting to climb. Through weeks 5 and 6, fatigue is often the first thing to arrive, and it can feel heavier than ordinary tiredness. Your breasts may feel sore, swollen, or tingly. You may need to pee more often, and certain smells, like coffee or cooking meat, can suddenly turn your stomach. None of this is required, though. Plenty of healthy pregnancies begin with barely a symptom, so a quiet start is not a warning sign on its own. Nausea often starts around week 6, and despite the name morning sickness, it can show up at any hour. Relief options deserve their own space, and they have a separate guide on this site, so the short version is this: nausea is common, it tends to ease by the second trimester, and having none does not mean anything is wrong. Mood swings are normal too, as are symptoms that come and go. A day with less nausea or softer breasts does not mean trouble. Early symptoms naturally fluctuate, and each pregnancy sets its own pattern. Your first prenatal appointment Call your clinic or midwife as soon as you have a positive test, because first appointments are typically scheduled for around 8 weeks. Some clinics see you earlier if you have a health condition, take regular medication, or have had complications before, so mention those when you call. Before the visit, note the first day of your last period, since dating starts from there. Pull together a list of your medications and supplements, your own health history, and any family history of conditions on either side. Ten minutes of preparation makes the appointment far more useful. The visit itself usually covers three things. First, a detailed history: your health, past pregnancies, medications, and lifestyle. Second, baseline tests, often including blood type, a blood count, immunity and infection screening, and a urine sample. Third, many clinics do a dating ultrasound to confirm how far along you are and check the heartbeat, though some schedule the scan separately. Bring questions. Keep a running list of dates, symptoms, and things you want to ask in BeMama or a notebook, because questions have a way of vanishing the moment someone asks if you have any. Small steps that matter right now Take 400 micrograms of folic acid every day if you are not already. ACOG and the CDC recommend it because the neural tube closes by about week 6, often before a first appointment, and folic acid lowers the risk of defects in that closure. Most prenatal vitamins contain at least this amount, so one daily prenatal usually covers it. Beyond that, eat what you can manage. Small, frequent meals are easier on an uneasy stomach than three large ones, and no single day of eating makes or breaks early pregnancy. Drink water steadily and rest when your body asks for it. Stop alcohol; no amount is known to be safe in pregnancy. If you smoke or vape, tell your clinician and ask for help quitting rather than trying to white-knuckle it alone. Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day, which is roughly one 12-ounce cup of coffee. Most importantly, do not stop a prescribed medication on your own. Many treatments are safe to continue, and stopping some of them abruptly is riskier than the medicine itself. Call the prescriber or a pharmacist, say you are pregnant, and ask what to do. That one phone call is often the most valuable step of the whole first trimester. When to call your clinician Some discomfort is expected. Mild cramping that feels like a light period, brief twinges on either side, and even light spotting can happen in a normal early pregnancy, especially around the time implantation finishes. Call your clinician the same day for bleeding that is more than light spotting or cramping that feels stronger than a period. Seek emergency care right away for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, severe pain, pain that sits on one side, shoulder-tip pain, or dizziness and fainting. These can signal an ectopic pregnancy, which needs immediate assessment. Calling does not commit you to anything. It simply gets an experienced person looking at your specific situation early, which is exactly what early care is for. Also call if you cannot keep fluids down for around 24 hours, if you feel faint or notice much darker urine, or if you have a fever or burning when you pee. Persistent vomiting has effective treatments, and dehydration is worth catching early. Finally, remember what an article can and cannot do. This guide describes what is typical; it cannot see your history or examine you. If something feels wrong to you, that feeling alone is a good enough reason to call. Clinics expect these calls from newly pregnant patients and would far rather hear from you early than late. By 8 weeks your baby has grown from poppy seed size to about 1.5 cm, roughly a kidney bean. Fatigue, breast tenderness, and nausea often start around week 6 and vary from day to day. The first prenatal visit usually happens around 8 weeks and includes history, baseline labs, and often a dating ultrasound. Take 400 mcg of folic acid daily and review medications with a clinician before changing anything. Seek emergency care for heavy bleeding or severe one-sided pain, and call your clinic if you cannot keep fluids down for 24 hours. What happens at 6 weeks pregnant? At 6 weeks, the neural tube that becomes the brain and spinal cord is closing, and cardiac activity can often be seen on a transvaginal ultrasound. The embryo is around the size of a lentil. For you, this is also when fatigue, breast tenderness, and nausea most commonly begin. How big is baby at 8 weeks? At 8 weeks, your baby measures about 1.5 cm, roughly the size of a kidney bean. Arm and leg buds are lengthening, facial features are forming, and the embryo is already moving, although you will not feel movement for several more months. Is cramping at 6 weeks pregnant normal? Mild cramping at 6 weeks is common and usually normal as your uterus grows and stretches. It often feels like a light period. Seek emergency care right away if cramping is severe or sits on one side, or if it comes with heavy bleeding, dizziness, or shoulder-tip pain, since those signs can mean an ectopic pregnancy and need immediate assessment. When is the first prenatal appointment? The first prenatal appointment usually happens around 8 weeks of pregnancy. Call your clinic as soon as you have a positive test, because schedules fill up, and mention any health conditions or regular medications, since those may mean you are seen earlier.

title: 9 to 12 Weeks Pregnant: Symptoms, Screening, Baby Growth
description: What happens between 9 and 12 weeks pregnant: how your baby grows from grape to lime size, why nausea peaks then fades, and when NIPT and the nuchal scan happen.
body: At 12 weeks pregnant, your baby measures about 5 to 6 cm from crown to rump, roughly the size of a lime, and every major organ has formed and is now busy growing. The stretch from week 9 to week 12 also covers the official shift from embryo to fetus, the usual peak of nausea, and the first big screening decisions, with NIPT possible from 10 weeks and the nuchal translucency scan at about 11 to 13 weeks. Here is what is happening, how you might feel, and what is worth doing before these windows close. From embryo to fetus: what changes in weeks 9 to 12 Around week 10, your baby graduates from embryo to fetus. The new name marks a real milestone: every major organ and body system has formed, and the work from here is growth and maturing rather than building from scratch. The size change across these weeks is striking. At week 9, your baby is about the size of a grape. By week 12, the crown to rump measurement is roughly 5 to 6 cm, about the size of a lime. The head still looks large compared with the body, which is normal at this stage, and the proportions slowly even out over the months ahead. A lot is happening in the details. Fingers and toes have separated, and tiny nails are starting to form. The intestines, which developed partly inside the umbilical cord, are moving into the abdomen. The kidneys begin producing urine, and the baby swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid. There is real movement too: stretching, flexing, even hiccup-like motions, although the baby is far too small for you to feel any of it yet. Near the end of this stretch, the placenta takes over most hormone production from the ovary, one reason many early symptoms begin to ease as you approach the second trimester. How you might feel right now For many people, nausea peaks somewhere around weeks 9 to 10 and then slowly loosens its grip between weeks 12 and 14. That timing is an average, not a promise. Some feel better sooner, some carry queasiness into the second trimester, and some never had it at all, which is also normal. Fatigue can be heavy through these weeks, the kind that makes an early bedtime feel non-negotiable. Food aversions and a sharp sense of smell are common, and bloating can make your waistband tight long before there is a true bump. If you want practical relief ideas, our guide to easing pregnancy nausea covers them in depth. You may also notice sore breasts, more saliva than usual, constipation, mild headaches, and mood swings that arrive without warning. Hormone levels are still climbing, and carrying a big secret while feeling unwell is genuinely tiring, so be patient with yourself. One quiet worry deserves a mention: some people panic when symptoms fade around week 11 or 12, but easing nausea at this stage usually reflects the normal hormonal shift, not a problem. Symptoms are a rough signal at best. If something feels wrong to you, or if vomiting is so constant that fluids will not stay down, contact your clinic rather than waiting it out. Screening decisions: NIPT and the nuchal scan Weeks 9 to 12 open the main first-trimester screening window, and the timing matters. Cell-free DNA screening, usually called NIPT, is a blood draw available from 10 weeks onward that screens for the most common chromosomal conditions. The nuchal translucency scan, an ultrasound that measures fluid at the back of the baby's neck, is done at about 11 to 13 weeks and is often combined with blood work as first-trimester combined screening. These are screening tests: they estimate chance, they do not give a diagnosis. What each test measures and how to read the results are covered in our guide to pregnancy blood tests and screening. Screening is a choice, not a requirement. Some people want as much information as early as possible, others prefer to skip optional tests, and both are reasonable. It helps to decide before the window arrives, because the nuchal scan cannot be done accurately after about 13 to 14 weeks. Useful questions for your clinic: which screens do you offer, what do they cost or does insurance cover them, how long do results take, and what would the next step be after a higher-chance result. Talk it through with your partner or a support person if the decision feels heavy. There is no single right answer, only the one that fits you. Hearing the heartbeat At a prenatal visit, a handheld doppler can often pick up the heartbeat somewhere around 10 to 12 weeks. Often is the honest word. Whether it works at a given visit depends on the position of the uterus and placenta, your body build, and how far along you actually are, since dating can be off by several days. Not finding the heartbeat with a doppler at this stage is common and is not, by itself, a sign that something is wrong. When a clinician cannot find it and wants reassurance, an ultrasound gives a much clearer answer, and many clinics move straight to one rather than searching for long. Home dopplers deserve a careful word. They are easy to buy and hard to use well. Untrained ears often mistake the mother's own pulse or blood flow through the placenta for the baby's heartbeat, which can give false reassurance when something needs attention, or false alarm when everything is fine. Most maternity guidance suggests leaving doppler checks to trained clinicians for exactly this reason. If you are worried between appointments, especially about bleeding, pain, or a sudden change in how you feel, call your clinic and describe the symptoms. A short phone conversation with someone qualified is worth more than an hour of anxious searching with a device at home. Your to-do list, and when to call A few tasks are genuinely time-sensitive right now. If you want the nuchal translucency scan, book it early, because the measurement window closes at about 13 to 14 weeks and appointment slots fill. Decide whether you want NIPT, and if so, arrange the blood draw any time from 10 weeks. If you have not had a first prenatal visit, schedule one. This is also when many people plan how to share the news. Waiting until after 12 weeks or the first scan is common, but there is no rule; a good test is to tell the people you would want support from if anything changed. Jot dates, symptoms, and questions in BeMama or a notebook so nothing gets lost. Some symptoms need a same-day call to your clinic, whatever the hour: bleeding heavier than light spotting, cramping that keeps getting worse, a fever of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, or burning when you urinate. So does vomiting that will not let fluids stay down, especially with signs of dehydration like dark urine or lightheadedness, since treatment can help and nobody should simply endure it. A smaller set of symptoms means emergency care right away rather than waiting for a callback: severe or one-sided belly pain, pain with dizziness, fainting, or shoulder-tip pain, or bleeding that soaks a pad within an hour, because these can signal internal bleeding that must be checked immediately. Light spotting on its own is common in early pregnancy and often harmless, but mention it at your next visit; when you are unsure which category you are in, call, because triage nurses answer exactly these questions all day. Around week 10 your baby officially becomes a fetus, and by week 12 measures about 5 to 6 cm, the size of a lime. Nausea often peaks near weeks 9 to 10 and eases for many people between weeks 12 and 14. NIPT is possible from 10 weeks, and the nuchal translucency scan happens at about 11 to 13 weeks. A doppler often finds the heartbeat around 10 to 12 weeks, but not always, and that alone is not alarming. Call your clinic the same day for heavy bleeding, worsening cramps, fever, or vomiting that keeps fluids from staying down; severe one-sided pain with dizziness or shoulder pain means emergency care. When can you get NIPT testing? NIPT, the cell-free DNA blood test, can be done any time from 10 weeks of pregnancy onward. There is no late cutoff, so you can also choose it after the first trimester if you decide later. It is a screening test that estimates the chance of common chromosomal conditions, not a diagnosis, so a higher-chance result would be followed by confirmatory testing. When does morning sickness peak? Nausea most often peaks around weeks 9 to 10 and starts easing between weeks 12 and 14. The pattern varies a lot from person to person, and some people stay queasy well into the second trimester. Contact your clinician if vomiting keeps you from holding down fluids, because effective treatment exists and you do not have to wait it out. What week is the nuchal translucency scan done? The nuchal translucency scan is done at about 11 to 13 weeks of pregnancy. The measurement is only accurate inside that window, so it helps to book early once your clinic offers it. It is often paired with a blood test as first-trimester combined screening, and like all screening it is optional. When can you hear the heartbeat with a doppler? A clinician can often find the heartbeat with a handheld doppler around 10 to 12 weeks, though sometimes not until a little later. The position of the uterus and placenta, body build, and dating that is off by a few days all affect it. Not hearing it at this stage is common and not by itself a warning sign; an ultrasound can confirm quickly if reassurance is needed.

title: 13 to 16 Weeks Pregnant: Second Trimester Start Guide
description: What to expect from 13 to 16 weeks pregnant: how your baby grows, which symptoms ease or begin, the tests offered in this window, and when to call your clinician.
body: At 16 weeks pregnant, your baby is about the size of an avocado, and many parents notice more energy, less nausea, and the first round ligament twinges as the uterus rises out of the pelvis. Weeks 13 to 16 are the opening stretch of the second trimester, a window when appointments settle into a rhythm and a few optional tests come up. This guide walks through what is growing, how you might feel, and what is worth doing now. Your baby, from a lemon to an avocado At 13 weeks, your baby is about the size of a lemon, roughly 7 centimeters from head to bottom. Over the next few weeks that length nearly doubles. At 14 weeks the kidneys are producing urine, the neck is lengthening, and facial muscles are starting to work, so your baby can squint and grimace. Fine, soft hair called lanugo begins to cover the skin, and the arms grow to a length that better matches the body. None of this is visible from the outside yet, which can feel strange. Growth in this window is fast, steady, and mostly quiet. By 15 to 16 weeks, your baby is about the size of an avocado, around 11 to 12 centimeters from crown to rump. Sucking motions begin, a rehearsal for feeding later. The ears have moved close to their final position, and the eyes have begun to make slow movements even though the eyelids stay fused. On an ultrasound around this time, the sex may be visible, although position and image quality decide whether the sonographer can say anything with confidence. Some parents feel the first faint flutters near 16 weeks, but many feel nothing until 18 to 22 weeks, especially in a first pregnancy. Both are normal. How you might feel from week 13 to 16 For many people, this stretch is when pregnancy finally starts to feel easier. Nausea fades for a large share of parents somewhere between 13 and 16 weeks, appetite comes back, and energy often returns as first trimester exhaustion lifts. The shift is real but not universal. Some people stay queasy into the second trimester, and a smaller group deals with nausea for much longer. If you are still vomiting often, cannot keep fluids down, or are losing weight, tell your clinician rather than waiting for it to pass. There is treatment for persistent nausea, and asking for it is not a failure. New sensations arrive as your uterus rises up and out of the pelvis. Round ligament pain often starts in this window: quick, sharp twinges low in the belly or groin when you stand, cough, sneeze, or roll over in bed. It is common and usually brief, and our round ligament pain guide covers relief in detail. You may also notice a firmer lower belly, nasal stuffiness, gum tenderness, and mild lightheadedness when you get up quickly, all tied to extra blood flow. A visible bump follows its own schedule, which our guide on when you start showing explains, so try not to compare yourself with others. Appointments and tests in this window Prenatal visits usually settle into a rhythm of roughly every four weeks through the middle of pregnancy, as long as things are going smoothly. Expect the basics at each visit: blood pressure, weight, urine checks, and listening to the fetal heartbeat with a handheld Doppler. These weeks sit just after the first trimester screening window, so if you had that testing, this is often when results are discussed. Because the second trimester officially begins around this point, a topic our trimesters guide covers, many clinics also use these visits to plan the rest of your testing calendar. Bring questions written down; short visits go faster than expected. Two tests belong to this stretch. The quad screen, a blood test that estimates the chance of neural tube defects and certain chromosomal conditions, including Down syndrome, is offered between about 15 and 22 weeks, and many clinics aim for 16 to 18 weeks. It is optional, and it is a screening test, not a diagnosis. Amniocentesis, when it is indicated by screening results, family history, or your own preference after counseling, is usually performed between about 15 and 20 weeks. If either test is on your mind, raise it at your next visit so the calendar does not decide for you. Good things to do between 13 and 16 weeks Book the anatomy scan now if your clinic has not already scheduled it. This detailed ultrasound usually happens between 18 and 22 weeks, and appointment slots can fill early, especially if you want a particular day or time. It is also a sensible moment to plan travel. Many people find the middle weeks of pregnancy the most comfortable for a trip: nausea has often faded, the bump is still small, and energy is better. Check your travel insurance, pack a copy of your prenatal records, and ask your clinician about anything specific to the destination, such as long flights, altitude, or food and water safety. If energy is returning, put some of it into gentle movement such as walking, swimming, or prenatal yoga; our safe exercise guide covers what to choose and what to skip. This is also a good window for unglamorous logistics: check parental leave paperwork deadlines, start a short list of questions for the anatomy scan, and note symptoms or dates somewhere you will actually find them later, whether that is a notebook or the BeMama app. Small habits started now, like a consistent bedtime and a water bottle you refill all day, tend to matter more in the third trimester than any single burst of preparation. When to call your clinician Call promptly for bleeding that is more than light spotting, fluid leaking from the vagina, a fever of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, severe or one-sided abdominal pain, pain or burning when you urinate, or vomiting that keeps you from holding down fluids. These signs do not automatically mean something is wrong, but each one deserves a same-day conversation rather than a search engine. Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, severe pain that does not ease, fainting, or trouble breathing calls for emergency care right away, not a message and a wait. If you notice spotting after sex or a pelvic exam, mention that too; it is often harmless, and your clinician can tell you what to watch for. Save the office number and the after-hours line in your phone now, before you need them. Mood deserves the same attention as physical symptoms. Relief and excitement often grow in these weeks, but anxiety, low mood, or intrusive worry can grow too, and pregnancy hormones are not a reason to dismiss them. Tell your clinician if sadness or worry fills most of the day for more than two weeks, disturbs your sleep beyond ordinary discomfort, or makes it hard to eat or function. Support ranges from talk therapy to medication that can be used in pregnancy, and any thoughts of harming yourself deserve immediate help from a crisis line or your care team, not a wait for the next appointment. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis; your own care team knows your history and is the right place for personal answers. Your baby grows from about a lemon to an avocado between 13 and 16 weeks. Energy often returns and nausea fades for many people, but not for everyone. Round ligament twinges commonly begin as the uterus rises out of the pelvis. The quad screen is offered at about 15 to 22 weeks, and the anatomy scan should be booked for 18 to 22 weeks. Call your clinician the same day for bleeding, leaking fluid, or fever. How big is baby at 16 weeks? At 16 weeks, a baby is about the size of an avocado, roughly 11 to 12 centimeters from crown to rump and around 100 grams. Ultrasound measurements normally vary a little from these averages. A steady growth pattern over time matters more than any single number on a report. What weeks is the quad screen done? The quad screen is offered between about 15 and 22 weeks of pregnancy, and many clinics aim for 16 to 18 weeks. It is an optional blood test that estimates the chance of certain conditions rather than diagnosing them. If a result is flagged, your clinician will walk you through follow-up options such as detailed ultrasound or amniocentesis. When does round ligament pain start? Round ligament pain most often starts in the early second trimester, around 13 to 16 weeks, as the uterus rises out of the pelvis and its supporting ligaments stretch. The twinges are typically sharp, brief, and set off by sudden movement like standing, coughing, or rolling over. Pain that is severe, constant, or paired with bleeding or fever is not typical round ligament pain, so call your clinician. Do you feel better in the second trimester? Many people do feel better in the second trimester, with nausea fading, energy returning, and appetite improving, often somewhere between 13 and 16 weeks. The change is gradual rather than a switch flipping on a set day. If you still feel rough at 16 weeks, that is common too, and persistent vomiting or exhaustion is worth raising at your next visit.

title: 17 to 20 Weeks Pregnant: Movement and the Anatomy Scan
description: A calm guide to being 20 weeks pregnant and the weeks around it: how your baby grows from week 17 to 20, first movements, the anatomy scan, and what to do next.
body: At 20 weeks pregnant you are roughly halfway through a 40 week pregnancy, and your baby now measures about 25 cm from crown to heel and weighs around 300 g. The stretch from week 17 to week 20 brings two milestones most parents remember: the first flutters of movement and the anatomy scan. This guide walks through what is developing, how you might feel, and the short list of things worth doing now. How your baby grows from week 17 to 20 Between weeks 17 and 20, your baby roughly doubles in weight. By week 20, most babies measure about 25 cm from crown to heel, around 10 inches, and weigh close to 300 g, a little over 10 ounces. Part of the jump you see on growth charts is a change in how babies are measured: before 20 weeks, length is usually given from crown to rump, and after that from crown to heel, so the legs suddenly count. Underneath the numbers, steady work is happening. Fat is beginning to form under the skin, muscles are getting stronger, and the movements that once looked random on ultrasound are becoming smoother and more coordinated. Two protective layers now cover your baby's skin. Vernix is a creamy white coating that shields the skin from the surrounding amniotic fluid, and lanugo is a layer of fine, soft hair that helps hold the vernix in place. Both are normal, and most of each disappears before birth. Hearing is developing quickly in this window too. The inner ear structures are maturing, and many babies begin responding to muffled sounds from your body and, a little later, to voices from outside. Your baby also swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid, which is early practice for feeding, and cycles through sleep and wake periods that may not match yours at all. How you might feel right now Somewhere in this stretch, many people feel movement for the first time. Most notice it between 16 and 22 weeks, and it often comes later in a first pregnancy simply because the sensation is easy to miss. Early movement rarely feels like a kick. It is closer to flutters, bubbles, or light tapping that comes and goes, and it is easiest to catch when you are lying down quietly. An anterior placenta, one that sits at the front of the uterus, can cushion the feeling for a few more weeks. If you have felt nothing yet, that is common at this stage and not a sign that something is wrong. Your body is changing visibly now. The top of the uterus reaches about the level of your belly button around week 20, so the bump is usually hard to hide. Common symptoms in this window include backache as your posture shifts, brief sharp twinges low in the belly when you stand or twist, known as round ligament pain, a stuffy nose, leg cramps at night, and skin changes such as a dark line down the belly or darker patches on the face. Appetite often picks up, and many people have more energy than they did in the first trimester. Comfortable shoes, regular snacks, and side sleeping with a pillow between your knees all start earning their keep. The anatomy scan, this window's headline appointment The headline appointment in this window is the anatomy scan, sometimes called the mid-pregnancy ultrasound or the 20 week scan. It is usually done between 18 and 22 weeks. A sonographer takes a long, careful look at how your baby is growing and checks the major organs and structures, from the brain and heart to the spine and limbs, in more detail than earlier scans could. The scan also looks at what surrounds your baby, including where the placenta is attached and how much amniotic fluid is present. It is a screening scan, which means it looks for anything that deserves a closer look. It is not a final verdict on your baby's health. For many parents this is also the moment they can learn their baby's sex, if the position cooperates and if they want to know. Tell the sonographer at the start if you would rather keep it a surprise. Plan for the appointment to take a while, often 30 to 45 minutes, and follow your clinic's instructions about arriving with a full bladder. Babies do not always pose helpfully, so being asked to walk around, or to return another day for repeat views, is common and usually means nothing more than an awkward angle. Your clinic will talk you through the findings and arrange any follow-up that is needed. Is 20 weeks really the halfway point? Twenty weeks is the halfway point in the way pregnancy is usually counted: 40 weeks from the first day of your last period. It is a fair milestone, but hold it loosely. Term is a window rather than a single date, and most babies arrive sometime between 37 and 42 weeks, so your second half may run a little shorter or longer than the first. If your due date was adjusted after an early ultrasound, use your clinic's dating rather than your own calendar math. However you count it, this is a natural moment to look up from week by week symptoms and start thinking about the months ahead. A short list beats a long one. First, book the anatomy scan if it is not already scheduled, because the 18 to 22 week window passes quickly. Second, start a low-effort movement habit: simply notice when your baby tends to be active, such as after meals or in the evening. There is no need to count anything yet, since formal kick counting belongs to the third trimester. Third, look into childbirth classes now, because popular ones fill up and many run across several weeks. This is also a reasonable time to ask about maternity or parental leave paperwork at work, while there is no urgency behind the question. Comfort, self-care, and when to call Small comforts matter more as the bump grows. Side sleeping with a pillow between your knees eases back strain, and rolling to your side before getting up from bed protects the round ligaments. Keep water nearby, keep snacks simple and regular, and use an unscented moisturizer if the skin over your belly feels itchy as it stretches. Gentle exercise such as walking or swimming is encouraged for most people; check with your clinician if you have been told to limit activity. It also helps to keep a running list of questions for the scan appointment. A notebook works well, or you can note dates, symptoms, and questions in the BeMama app so they are ready when you need them. At this stage, no one expects you to monitor movement formally, and a quiet day is not yet something clinicians ask you to track. Some symptoms should be reported promptly at any stage, though. Call your maternity team right away, rather than waiting for your next appointment, for vaginal bleeding, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, a severe or persistent headache, changes in your vision, a fever, pain or burning when you pass urine, or strong cramping that does not settle with rest. None of these automatically means something is wrong, but each deserves a real conversation rather than a search engine, and your team would much rather hear about a symptom early than have you wait and worry. By week 20 your baby measures about 25 cm from crown to heel and weighs around 300 g. First movements are usually felt between 16 and 22 weeks, and often later in a first pregnancy. The anatomy scan happens between 18 and 22 weeks and checks growth, organs, and placenta position. Twenty weeks is roughly halfway through a standard 40 week pregnancy, so it is a good moment to book classes and plan ahead. Report bleeding, leaking fluid, severe headache, vision changes, or fever to your clinician promptly at any stage. When do you first feel the baby kick? Most people first feel movement between 16 and 22 weeks of pregnancy. In a first pregnancy it often comes later in that window, because the early flutters are easy to mistake for gas or muscle twitches. An anterior placenta can also cushion the sensation for a few extra weeks. Feeling nothing yet at 17 to 20 weeks is common and usually normal. What week is the anatomy scan done? The anatomy scan is usually done between 18 and 22 weeks of pregnancy, most often around week 20. It is a detailed ultrasound that checks your baby's growth and major organs, along with the placenta's position and the amount of amniotic fluid. If yours is not booked yet, contact your clinic soon, because the window is fairly narrow. Is 20 weeks halfway through pregnancy? Yes, 20 weeks is roughly the halfway point, because pregnancy is usually counted as 40 weeks from the first day of your last period. In practice the second half varies, since most babies arrive somewhere between 37 and 42 weeks. Treat it as a milestone rather than an exact countdown. What happens at 18 weeks pregnant? At 18 weeks your baby is about 14 cm from crown to rump and weighs around 200 g, the ears are settling into position, and hearing is developing. Many people feel the first flutters of movement around this week, though feeling them later is still normal. It is also the earliest week many clinics book the anatomy scan.

title: 21 to 24 Weeks Pregnant: Baby Growth and Viability
description: What to expect from 21 to 24 weeks pregnant: how your baby grows to viability, common symptoms like Braxton Hicks, and the appointments and to-dos for this window.
body: At 24 weeks pregnant, your baby is about 30 cm long, weighs around 600 g, just over a pound, and has reached the milestone many clinicians call viability. Weeks 21 to 24 bring stronger daily kicks, possibly your first Braxton Hicks contractions, and a few new items for the calendar, including the glucose screen. This guide walks through what is developing, what you may feel, and what is worth doing now. How your baby grows from week 21 to 24 Between weeks 21 and 24, your baby puts on weight quickly, gaining more than half again what they weighed at the start of this window. At 21 weeks, most babies weigh around 350 to 400 g and measure about 26 to 27 cm from head to heel. By 24 weeks, typical estimates are close to 600 g, just over a pound, and about 30 cm, roughly the length of an ear of corn. Fat is starting to build under the skin, which still looks thin and wrinkled. Movements are more coordinated now: stretching, kicking, turning, even grabbing the umbilical cord. Many parents begin to notice a loose pattern of active and quiet periods across the day. Two developments in this window matter a great deal. The lungs begin producing the early building blocks of surfactant, the substance that will eventually let the air sacs stay open after birth. That process continues for many weeks, which is one reason every extra week of pregnancy helps. Hearing also matures noticeably. Your baby can pick up your voice, your heartbeat, and louder sounds from outside, and may respond to them with a kick or a wriggle. Talking, reading, or singing is not required homework, but if it feels natural, this is the stage where your baby genuinely starts to listen. What viability at 24 weeks actually means You will often see 24 weeks described as the threshold of viability. In plain terms, it is the point where, if a baby were born extremely early, hospitals with a neonatal intensive care unit can usually offer full support, and survival becomes a realistic possibility. Chances improve meaningfully with every additional week after that. Exact outcomes vary by country, by hospital, and by the baby's own condition, so no single number applies to everyone. Some hospitals also consider active care slightly earlier in specific situations, a decision made case by case together with the family. It helps to hold this milestone lightly. The vast majority of pregnancies continue far beyond 24 weeks, and reaching this point is not a hint that anything is about to go wrong. Think of it as quiet reassurance in the background rather than a deadline you were racing toward. The practical use of the information is simple: know which nearby hospital has newborn intensive care, keep your maternity notes easy to find, and learn the signs of preterm labor covered below so you could act quickly in the unlikely event you ever needed to. How your body may feel in these weeks Kicks change character in this stretch. What felt like flutters becomes unmistakable thumps, and by 24 weeks many parents feel movement every day, often strongest in the evening or after meals. You do not need to count anything formally yet; just get familiar with what a normal day of movement feels like for your baby. You may also meet Braxton Hicks contractions for the first time. These are practice tightenings of the uterus: the bump goes hard for perhaps 30 to 60 seconds, then relaxes. They are irregular, usually painless, and often triggered by activity, a full bladder, or dehydration. Other common companions include leg cramps that strike at night, mild swelling in the ankles and feet by the end of the day, a heartier appetite, backache, and round ligament twinges when you stand up or roll over quickly. Gentle calf stretches before bed, steady water intake, putting your feet up, and supportive shoes take the edge off most of it. Swelling that is sudden, severe, or involves your face and hands is different: that deserves a same-day call to your clinician, because it can occasionally signal a blood pressure problem rather than ordinary pregnancy puffiness. Appointments and checks in this window From about 24 weeks, prenatal visits usually add a simple new measurement: fundal height. Your clinician or midwife runs a tape measure from the top of the pubic bone to the top of the uterus. In centimeters, the number roughly matches your week of pregnancy, give or take a couple of centimeters. It is a quick, low-tech way to confirm that growth is tracking as expected between ultrasounds. If the measurement runs noticeably ahead of or behind your dates, the usual next step is a growth ultrasound, which most of the time simply confirms that everything is fine. This is also the moment to get your glucose screen on the calendar. Most clinics order it for the 24 to 28 week window, so if no one has mentioned it yet, ask at your next visit and book a slot that suits your schedule. Some people also have follow-up imaging if the anatomy scan could not see everything, which is common and rarely a cause for worry. Between appointments, jot down questions in BeMama or on paper as they occur to you: sleep positions, travel plans, workplace adjustments. A short written list makes a fifteen-minute visit far more useful. Useful things to do before the third trimester Energy is often decent in this stretch, which makes it a good season for practical projects. Start or finish the baby registry, sketch out the nursery or sleeping arrangement, and compare parental leave dates with your partner or employer. None of it has to be finished this month, but spreading the work out beats a third-trimester scramble. Keep paying casual attention to movement, too. If your baby seems clearly quieter than usual for a day, lie down on your side and pay close attention for a while; if you are still not reassured, call your clinic the same day rather than waiting. Learn the signs of preterm labor now, while everything is calm. Call your clinic or maternity unit promptly if you notice contractions that come regularly and keep coming, perhaps four or more in an hour, a constant low backache that is new, strong pelvic or vaginal pressure, period-like cramping, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, or any bleeding. Do not wait overnight to see whether it settles, and do not worry about being wrong. Preterm labor can often be slowed or treated when it is caught early, and maternity staff would much rather check a false alarm than miss a real one. By 24 weeks your baby is about 30 cm long and just over a pound, with lungs and hearing developing fast. Viability at 24 weeks is background reassurance, not a deadline; most pregnancies continue far beyond it. Braxton Hicks are irregular, usually painless practice tightenings that pass with rest and water. Ask at your next visit to book the glucose screen for the 24 to 28 week window. Call your clinic promptly for regular tightening, pelvic pressure, leaking fluid, or bleeding. What symptoms are normal at 24 weeks pregnant? Strong daily kicks, Braxton Hicks tightenings, leg cramps, mild ankle swelling, backache, and a bigger appetite are all common at 24 weeks. Most ease with water, movement breaks, calf stretches, and putting your feet up. Sudden severe swelling, regular painful contractions, bleeding, or leaking fluid are not routine symptoms and deserve a same-day call to your clinician. Is a baby viable at 24 weeks? Yes, 24 weeks is the point most often cited as viability, meaning a baby born this early has a realistic chance of survival with neonatal intensive care. Outcomes vary with the baby's condition and the hospital's resources, and chances improve substantially with each further week. Birth this early is uncommon, so treat the milestone as reassurance rather than a prediction. When do Braxton Hicks contractions start? Many people first notice Braxton Hicks contractions in the second trimester, often somewhere around weeks 20 to 24, though some feel them earlier and some never notice them at all. They are irregular, usually painless tightenings that pass with rest, a drink of water, or a change of position. Contractions that become regular, painful, or persistent before 37 weeks should be reported to your clinic promptly. How big is a baby at 24 weeks? At 24 weeks a baby typically measures about 30 cm from head to heel and weighs around 600 g, a little over a pound, roughly the size of an ear of corn. Ultrasound estimates carry a margin of error, and healthy babies come in a range of sizes at every week. Your clinician watches the trend over time rather than any single number.

title: 25 to 28 Weeks Pregnant: Glucose Test and Third Trimester
description: What to expect from 25 to 28 weeks pregnant: how big your baby is at 28 weeks, the glucose test window, the Tdap and RhoGAM shots, and when to call.
body: At 28 weeks pregnant you are entering the third trimester: your baby weighs about 1 kilogram, roughly 2 to 2.5 pounds, measures around 35 to 37 centimeters, and their eyes have recently opened. Weeks 25 to 28 are the busiest testing stretch of pregnancy, with the glucose screen due, the Tdap window opening at 27 weeks, and a RhoGAM shot around week 28 for Rh negative parents. Visits also move to every two weeks from here. If you want a refresher on how trimesters are counted, our trimester guide covers that; this one sticks to what these four weeks feel like and what to get done. How your baby grows from week 25 to 28 Between weeks 25 and 28, your baby's eyes open for the first time, usually around week 26 to 28, and the eyelids begin to blink. The brain is growing quickly, and its surface starts to fold, packing in more surface area for everything it will do later. The lungs are maturing too. They produce a substance called surfactant that will help the air sacs stay open after birth, and your baby practices breathing movements with amniotic fluid. By week 28, most babies measure roughly 35 to 37 centimeters from head to heel and weigh about 1 kilogram, which is around 2 to 2.5 pounds. You may start to notice a rhythm to all this growing. Many babies develop clearer sleep and wake cycles in this stretch, so quiet spells and busy spells become easier to recognize. Hiccups can show up as small rhythmic taps that go on for a few minutes, and they are completely normal. Fat is slowly building under the skin, which smooths it out and will help with temperature control after birth. Your baby still has plenty of room to move, so do not worry about position yet. Many babies flip repeatedly for weeks before settling head down closer to the end. How you might feel right now Heartburn is one of the most common complaints in this stretch. Pregnancy hormones relax the valve at the top of the stomach while the growing uterus presses upward, so acid escapes more easily. Smaller meals, eating slowly, and staying upright for a while after food often help, and you can ask your clinician about antacids that are considered safe in pregnancy. Backache is common too, because your center of gravity shifts forward and ligaments loosen. Gentle stretching, supportive shoes, a warm shower, and a pillow between your knees at night can each take some of the pressure off. Sleep often gets harder before it gets better. Side sleeping with a pillow under your bump and another between your knees is a comfortable, commonly recommended setup. Kicks are vivid now, and you will probably notice active periods, often after meals or when you lie down at night. Some people also feel practice contractions called Braxton Hicks: irregular tightenings that ease with rest, a position change, or a glass of water. Leg cramps and mild ankle swelling at the end of the day are common as well. Sudden or severe swelling is different, and it is covered further down. Three tests share this window The glucose screen is due now if you have not had it yet. It is usually done between 24 and 28 weeks, and it checks how your body handles sugar during pregnancy, because gestational diabetes often causes no symptoms at all. If your clinic has not mentioned it by your next visit, ask about it directly. Our separate glucose test guide walks through the drink, the difference between the one hour and three hour versions, and what the results mean, so here the message is simple: get it on the calendar. It is one of the most useful routine checks in the whole pregnancy. Two shots may also come up. If your blood type is Rh negative, most clinicians recommend an injection of Rh immune globulin, often called RhoGAM, around 28 weeks. It stops your immune system from making antibodies against your baby's blood cells, which protects this pregnancy and future ones. Separately, the Tdap vaccine window opens at 27 weeks. The CDC recommends Tdap between 27 and 36 weeks of every pregnancy so your baby is born with some early protection against whooping cough. Our vaccine guide covers the details. For now, simply ask about both at your next appointment. Visits move to every two weeks From around week 28, prenatal visits typically move from once a month to every two weeks. Each visit is usually short: blood pressure, your baby's heartbeat, a belly measurement called fundal height, and time for your questions. The new rhythm can feel sudden, so it helps to book several appointments ahead while convenient time slots are still open. Write questions down as they occur to you during the week, because they have a way of vanishing in the exam room. No question is too small at this stage, including anything about symptoms, work, travel, or early thoughts on birth plans. This is also when daily movement starts to matter more. From about week 28, get to know your baby's normal: when the active periods happen, what they feel like, and roughly how busy a typical day is. There is no single magic number of kicks. The useful signal is a change from your own baby's usual pattern. Some clinicians suggest formal kick counting sessions, so it is worth asking whether they want you to do that and how. A quick note of active times in BeMama or a notebook makes it easier to spot a real change instead of guessing from memory. When to call your clinician Call right away if your baby's movements slow down or stop once you know their pattern. Do not wait until morning, and do not talk yourself out of it. Clinics expect these calls, checking is quick, and most calls end in reassurance. The same urgency applies to a severe headache that does not ease, vision changes such as blurring or flashing spots, sudden swelling of your face or hands, or pain high in your belly. These can signal a blood pressure problem, and our blood pressure and preeclampsia guide explains what clinicians look for in more depth. Call right away as well for regular painful tightenings before 37 weeks, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, or any bleeding. Fever, or pain and burning when you pee, deserve a same day call. None of these automatically means something is wrong, but each one is worth a professional opinion rather than a night of worrying. Save your clinic's daytime and after hours numbers in your phone now, before you need them. Your care team knows your history and would rather hear from you early. When in doubt, make the call. That is exactly what they are there for. By 28 weeks your baby weighs about 1 kilogram and measures roughly 35 to 37 centimeters. The glucose screen is usually done between 24 and 28 weeks, so book it if you have not already. The Tdap window opens at 27 weeks, and Rh negative parents usually get RhoGAM around week 28. Prenatal visits typically move to every two weeks starting around week 28. Call your clinician right away for decreased movement, severe headache, vision changes, or sudden swelling. What are common symptoms at 28 weeks pregnant? Common symptoms at 28 weeks include heartburn, backache, trouble sleeping, leg cramps, mild ankle swelling, and strong kicks with recognizable active periods. Irregular practice contractions called Braxton Hicks are also common and ease with rest or a change of position. Sudden severe swelling, a headache that will not ease, or vision changes are different: call your clinician right away for those. How big is a baby at 28 weeks? At 28 weeks, most babies weigh about 1 kilogram, roughly 2 to 2.5 pounds, and measure around 35 to 37 centimeters from head to heel. Healthy babies vary, so your own measurements may sit a little above or below these ranges. Your clinician tracks growth over time rather than judging any single number. What week is the glucose test in pregnancy? The glucose screen is usually done between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Some people are screened earlier if they have risk factors, and your clinic will tell you if that applies to you. Our separate glucose test guide explains the drink, the one hour and three hour versions, and what the results mean. When do you get the Tdap shot in pregnancy? The CDC recommends the Tdap vaccine between 27 and 36 weeks in every pregnancy, and earlier in that window gives your baby more time to receive protective antibodies before birth. The goal is early protection against whooping cough for your newborn. Ask about it at your next prenatal visit, and see our vaccine guide for more detail.

title: 29 to 32 Weeks Pregnant: Kick Counts and Rapid Growth
description: What to expect at 29 to 32 weeks pregnant: your baby's fastest growth stretch, common symptoms like breathlessness and heartburn, daily kick counts, and the appointments that matter now.
body: At 32 weeks pregnant, your baby usually weighs about 1.7 to 2 kg, close to 4 pounds, measures around 40 to 42 cm from head to heel, and is often settling head down. Weeks 29 to 32 are one of the fastest growth stretches of pregnancy, and you will likely feel it in your ribs, your bladder, and your sleep. Here is what is changing, what is normal to feel, and what to do about it. Your baby's fastest growth stretch Weeks 29 to 32 are the fastest weight-gain stretch of pregnancy. Your baby adds roughly 200 grams or more each week, moving from around 1.2 kg at week 29 to about 1.7 to 2 kg, close to 4 pounds, by week 32. Length reaches roughly 40 to 42 cm from head to heel. Much of the new weight is fat under the skin, which smooths out wrinkles and will help your baby hold a steady temperature after birth. You may notice the growth yourself: your bump rises higher, kicks land harder, and your appetite may swing between hungry and full after a few bites as space gets tight. Inside, the pace matches the scale. Bones are hardening, though the skull stays soft and flexible so the head can mold during birth. The lungs are maturing, and your baby practices breathing movements with amniotic fluid. The brain is growing quickly, and sleep cycles are becoming more organized, which is why you may notice active and quiet stretches at predictable times of day. Many babies begin settling head down during these weeks. If yours is still breech or lying sideways, there is no need to worry yet; most babies turn on their own before the final weeks, and your provider will keep checking position at each visit. How you might feel right now Feeling short of breath around 30 weeks is common and usually harmless. The top of your uterus now sits high enough to crowd your diaphragm, so your lungs have less room to expand even though you and your baby are getting plenty of oxygen. Slowing your pace, sitting tall, sleeping propped on pillows, and lifting your arms overhead for a moment can all ease it. Many people get relief later on, when the baby drops lower into the pelvis. Breathlessness that comes on suddenly, feels severe, or arrives with chest pain, a racing heart, or dizziness is different: seek emergency care right away, because these can be signs of a blood clot in the lung, which is rare but serious in pregnancy. Heartburn often flares in this stretch because the uterus presses on your stomach and pregnancy hormones relax the valve at the top of it. Smaller meals, staying upright after eating, and asking your provider about safe antacids can help. Pelvic pressure and a heavier feeling low in the belly are typical as the baby gains weight. You may also notice Braxton Hicks contractions: irregular tightenings that fade when you change position, walk, rest, or drink water. Sleep tends to fragment now between bathroom trips, a busy baby, and finding a comfortable position. Short daytime rests and an earlier wind-down help more than trying to force one long perfect night. Kick counts become part of the day From around week 28, many providers suggest a daily kick count, and weeks 29 to 32 are when the habit is worth locking in. A common method is simple: pick the same hour each day, ideally when your baby is usually active, such as after a meal. Settle on your side, start a timer, and note how long it takes to feel 10 movements. Kicks, rolls, swishes, and stretches all count; hiccups do not. Your provider may teach a slightly different method, and theirs is the one to follow. Jot the time in BeMama or on paper so a pattern builds; the record matters more than any single day. The point of counting is to learn your baby's normal, because every baby has its own rhythm. Some are busiest at night, others after breakfast. A change from that usual pattern matters more than any comparison with someone else's pregnancy. If movement seems reduced, slower, or different, contact your maternity unit or provider right away, even in the middle of the night. Do not wait until tomorrow, and do not rely on cold drinks or sugary snacks to wake the baby before calling; a prompt check is the reliable answer. Our separate guide to baby movement patterns covers counting methods and what changes can mean in more detail. Appointments, position checks, and the Tdap window Prenatal visits usually run every two weeks through this stretch. Expect the familiar basics: blood pressure, urine, your baby's heartbeat, and a fundal height measurement to track growth. Around now, providers also start feeling your belly to check which way the baby is lying, and they will keep doing this at every visit until birth. Bring your questions written down, because two-week gaps go fast. Good ones for this window: When should I call about contractions? What does your office want me to do about reduced movement after hours? When will we talk through my birth preferences? Short visits work better when you arrive with a short list. If you have not had the Tdap vaccine yet this pregnancy, this is the window: it is recommended between 27 and 36 weeks, and earlier in that range gives your body more time to pass protective antibodies to your baby before birth. Those antibodies help shield a newborn from whooping cough during the first months, before the baby's own vaccines begin. Ask at your next visit if it has not come up. This is also a good moment to ask which other seasonal vaccines, such as flu or RSV protection, are recommended where you live, since guidance depends on the season and your situation. Small to-dos, and when to call A few low-effort tasks now save stress later. Settle into sleeping on your side if you have not already; from the third trimester it is the position providers recommend, and our sleep positions guide covers the details. Tour your birth location, whether hospital or birth center, and learn where to park, which entrance is open at night, and where to check in. If you have older children or pets, sketch a plan for who covers them when labor starts, including a backup. Keep water and snacks within reach at your desk and bedside. None of this needs to be finished this week; one small task per weekend is enough. Keep the call-now list somewhere easy to find. Contact your provider or maternity unit right away, at any hour, for reduced or changed fetal movement. Call promptly for a headache that will not ease, especially with vision changes such as flashing lights or blurring, or sudden swelling of your face or hands; these can be signs of a blood pressure problem that needs checking. Also call for regular painful tightenings before 37 weeks, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, bleeding, fever, or pain when you pee. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis, and your care team would rather hear from you early than have you wait and worry at home. By week 32, most babies weigh about 1.7 to 2 kg and many are settling head down. Breathlessness, heartburn, pelvic pressure, and Braxton Hicks are all common in these weeks. Start a daily kick count at the same hour each day, and call right away if movement drops. Visits move to every two weeks, and Tdap belongs in the 27 to 36 week window. A headache with vision changes or sudden swelling of your face or hands needs a prompt call. How big is my baby at 32 weeks? At 32 weeks, babies typically weigh about 1.7 to 2 kg, close to 4 pounds, and measure roughly 40 to 42 cm from head to heel. Growth is fast right now, at roughly 200 grams or more per week, and much of it is the fat that helps newborns stay warm after birth. Your provider tracks this with fundal height measurements and, when needed, an ultrasound. When should I start counting kicks? Most providers suggest starting daily kick counts around week 28, so weeks 29 to 32 are the time to make it routine if you have not begun. Pick the same hour each day, rest on your side, and time how long it takes to feel 10 movements. Follow your own provider's method if they teach a different one, and call right away, even at night, if movement seems reduced. Is shortness of breath normal at 30 weeks pregnant? Yes, mild breathlessness around 30 weeks is common because the growing uterus crowds the diaphragm and leaves the lungs less room to expand. Slowing down, sitting tall, and sleeping propped up usually help, and many people breathe easier once the baby drops lower into the pelvis. Sudden or severe shortness of breath, or breathlessness with chest pain, a racing heart, or dizziness, is different: seek emergency care right away. Should my baby be head down at 32 weeks? Many babies settle head down by around 32 weeks, but plenty are still breech or sideways at this point, and most turn on their own in the following weeks. Position is not fixed yet, so a breech finding now is information, not a problem to solve today. Your provider will keep checking at each visit and will discuss options only if the baby stays breech closer to term.

title: 33 to 36 Weeks Pregnant: GBS Test and Getting Ready
description: What to expect from 33 to 36 weeks pregnant: your baby's growth, common symptoms, the group B strep test, weekly prenatal visits, and a calm get-ready checklist.
body: At 36 weeks pregnant, your baby is roughly 47 cm long and weighs about 2.5 to 3 kg, prenatal visits usually move to a weekly schedule, and the group B strep swab is done between 36 and 37 weeks. The month from week 33 to week 36 is the getting-ready stretch: your baby's lungs near maturity, your body starts rehearsing, and the practical to-do list finally gets short enough to finish. This guide walks through what changes, which appointments anchor these weeks, and what deserves a call to your clinician. How your baby grows from week 33 to 36 Between weeks 33 and 36, your baby moves from busy practice to near readiness. At 33 weeks, many babies measure around 43 cm from head to heel and weigh close to 2 kg. By 36 weeks, that has often grown to roughly 47 cm and 2.5 to 3 kg, about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds. The lungs are close to mature, and most babies born after this window breathe well, though some still need short-term support.
