At the breast this happens naturally, and with a bottle it means pausing when the sucking slows and stopping when your baby turns away, even if milk is left. Coaxing a full baby to finish a bottle teaches them to ignore their own signals and often ends in spit-up. If you worry about intake, judge it over days, not single feeds: steady weight gain at checkups and plenty of wet and dirty diapers tell the real story, and our diaper output guide covers what to expect there. Jot feed times in the BeMama app or a notebook if seeing the pattern helps you relax. Sleepy newborns: when to wake for a feed Most newborns feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, and the gaps are rarely even. Breastfed babies usually land near the top of that range, while formula-fed babies often go a little longer between feeds. In the first days many babies are very sleepy and will not reliably wake themselves to eat. Until your baby has regained their birth weight and is gaining steadily, pediatric guidance is to wake them for a feed about every 3 to 4 hours, counted from the start of one feed to the start of the next. After weight gain is established and your clinician agrees, you can usually let a healthy baby set the schedule at night while still feeding on cue during the day. To wake a sleepy feeder, start gently and escalate. Unwrap the swaddle and undress your baby down to the diaper, since cool skin rouses better than warmth. Change the diaper, hold your baby skin to skin, stroke the soles of the feet, sit them upright supported in your hands, and dim the lights so their eyes are willing to open. Talk to them as you go. Call your clinician the same day if your baby is hard to wake for feeds, cannot stay awake long enough to feed well, is breastfeeding fewer than about 8 times in 24 hours in the early weeks, seems unusually floppy, has fewer wet diapers than expected, or looks more yellow than the day before. A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher in a newborn needs medical attention right away. Feed at early cues like rooting, hand sucking, and lip smacking, before fussing starts. Crying is a late hunger cue, so calm your baby before offering the breast or bottle. Most newborns feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, usually at uneven intervals. Fullness looks like slowing sucks, relaxed open hands, and turning away from the nipple. Wake a sleepy newborn about every 3 to 4 hours until birth weight is regained, and call your clinician if your baby is hard to wake. How often should a newborn eat? Most newborns eat 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, which averages out to roughly every 2 to 3 hours but rarely follows a tidy pattern. Some feeds bunch close together and others spread out. Formula-fed babies often go a little longer between feeds than breastfed babies. Follow your baby's cues rather than the clock, and expect the rhythm to shift from week to week. If your breastfed newborn regularly feeds fewer than about 8 times a day in the early weeks, or any newborn keeps sleeping through feeds, check in with your clinician. Is crying a late hunger cue? Yes, crying is a late hunger cue, and by that point a newborn is often too upset to latch or take a bottle well. Calm your baby first with holding, skin to skin contact, and a quiet voice, then offer the feed. Aiming to feed at earlier cues, like rooting and hands moving to the mouth, makes most feeds smoother. Should I wake my newborn to feed? Yes, in the early weeks a newborn who has not yet regained their birth weight should be woken to feed about every 3 to 4 hours. Sleepy newborns do not always wake themselves for the calories they need. Once weight gain is steady and your pediatric clinician agrees, you can usually let your baby wake on their own at night. What does it mean when my baby is rooting? Rooting means your baby turns their head toward a touch on the cheek and opens their mouth, and it is one of the earliest hunger cues. It is a built-in newborn reflex that helps a baby find the breast or bottle. Rooting right after a full feed does not always signal hunger, since the reflex can fire from any cheek touch, but frequent rooting between feeds is a clear invitation to offer milk.

title: How to Get a Good Latch: Step by Step for Newborns
description: Learn how to get a good latch step by step: positioning, the wide gape, chin-first attachment, signs of a good latch, and how to fix a shallow, painful latch.
body: To get a good latch, hold your baby tummy to tummy, line their nose up with your nipple, wait for their mouth to open wide like a yawn, then bring them to the breast chin first so they take a deep mouthful of breast, not just the nipple. A deep latch is what makes feeding comfortable for you and effective for your baby. Most early pain comes from a shallow latch, and most shallow latches improve when you reset the same few steps. Set up the position before the latch Start before the latch. Sit or lie somewhere with back support, and bring your baby to your body rather than hunching toward them. Turn your baby fully onto their side so their chest rests against yours, tummy to tummy, with their ear, shoulder, and hip in one straight line. A baby who has to turn their head to reach the breast cannot swallow well, the same way it is hard for you to drink with your chin on your shoulder. Use a pillow or a rolled towel under your arm if your shoulders start creeping up toward your ears. Line your baby's nose up with your nipple, not their mouth. This looks slightly off target, and that is the point: it encourages them to tip their head back and reach up with an open mouth, which sets up a deep latch. Support them across the shoulders and the base of the head with your hand or forearm, and leave the back of the head free. Pushing on the head makes most babies push back and clamp down. Hold your breast if it helps, with your fingers well behind the areola in a C shape so they do not get in the way of the latch. The latch, step by step With the nose lined up, brush your nipple from your baby's nose down toward their upper lip and wait. You are waiting for a wide gape, a mouth open like a yawn, with the tongue down and forward. It can take a few passes, and that is normal. When the mouth opens wide, move quickly and bring your baby to the breast, not the breast to the baby. Their chin and lower jaw should touch the breast first, well below the nipple, while the head tips back slightly. The nipple then rolls in last, pointing toward the roof of the mouth. Aim for an asymmetric latch. That means your baby takes a big mouthful of breast, with more of the areola covered below the nipple than above it. You may see more of the darker skin above their top lip than below their chin, and that is exactly what you want. If the latch lands right on the tip of the nipple, it will feel pinchy and shallow. Do not try to push through it or wiggle the baby deeper on. Slip a clean finger into the corner of their mouth to release the suction, take a breath, and start the sequence again from the wide gape. What a good latch looks and feels like Check the picture from the outside. In a good latch, your baby's chin is pressed into the breast and their nose is free or just touching. Both lips are flanged outward like a fish, not tucked in. Their cheeks look full and rounded rather than dimpled or sucked in. Their mouth covers a wide stretch of breast, not just the nipple, and their head is tipped slightly back. You should not see the nipple slipping in and out, and you should not hear clicking or smacking sounds, which can mean the seal is breaking. Listen and feel. After the first minute or two of quick sucks, the rhythm usually slows into deeper draws, and once milk is flowing you may hear or see soft swallows, a quiet sound or a brief pause of the jaw. The first few seconds can pinch, especially in the early weeks, but the feeling should ease quickly into a strong tugging that does not hurt. When your baby comes off, your nipple should look roughly the same shape it went in, maybe a little longer, but not creased, flattened, or angled like a new lipstick. That wedge shape is a classic sign of a shallow latch. Fixing a shallow latch, and when baby will not latch If it hurts, take the latch apart and start again. Never pull your baby straight off, because the suction is strong and pulling can damage skin. Slide a clean finger into the corner of their mouth between the gums until the seal releases, then bring them off gently. Reset the basics before trying again: tummy to tummy, nose to nipple, wait for the wide gape, chin first. Small changes make a big difference, so try shifting your baby's body a little lower on your chest so they have to reach up, or hugging their bottom in closer so the head naturally tips back. If your newborn will not latch at all, lower the pressure before you troubleshoot technique. A frantic, crying baby cannot organize a latch, so calm them first with skin to skin contact, your chest bare and your baby in just a diaper. Many newborns start rooting and attach themselves from this position, especially in a laid-back posture where gravity holds them against you. Hand expressing a few drops of milk onto the nipple can spark interest. If your baby is very sleepy, offer the breast at the first flutter of waking instead of waiting for full cries. Keep attempts short and calm, and take breaks rather than forcing it. When to ask for skilled help Some tenderness while you both learn is common in the first week or two, but ongoing pain is a signal, not a rite of passage. Contact your midwife, health visitor, pediatric office, or a board certified lactation consultant, often called an IBCLC, if pain lasts through whole feeds, if nipples are cracked, bleeding, or coming out creased and white, or if you hear clicking at most feeds. The same goes if your baby seems unsettled after most feeds, has fewer wet diapers than expected, meaning fewer than about six heavy ones a day once your milk increases around day five, or is not gaining weight at checkups. Latch problems are usually fixable, and hands-on adjustments from a skilled helper often work faster than weeks of guessing alone. Asking for help is normal, not a failure. Feeding is a skill two people learn together, and clinicians expect questions in the early weeks. Before an appointment, jot down when the pain happens, what the nipple looks like afterward, and what you have already tried. You can keep those notes in the BeMama app or on paper so the details are ready when someone asks. Seek care promptly for possible mastitis: a hard, red, painful area of the breast along with fever or flu-like feelings. And call your baby's clinician right away, not just at the next checkup, if your baby is hard to wake for feeds, seems floppy or unusually weak, or has gone many hours without a wet diaper. Hold your baby tummy to tummy with their nose lined up to your nipple. Wait for a wide open mouth, then bring your baby to the breast chin first. A good latch shows flanged lips, rounded cheeks, and comfort after the first few seconds. Break suction with a clean finger and relatch instead of pushing through pain. Persistent pain, damaged nipples, or clicking sounds deserve skilled help, such as an IBCLC. What does a good latch look like? In a good latch, your baby's chin touches the breast, both lips are flanged outward, the cheeks look rounded, and the mouth covers a wide stretch of areola, more below the nipple than above. Once milk flows you may hear soft, rhythmic swallowing. Any pinching should ease within the first few seconds, and the nipple should come out its normal shape rather than creased or flattened. Why does breastfeeding hurt? Breastfeeding usually hurts because the latch is shallow, so the nipple gets compressed near the front of the mouth instead of resting deep inside. Brief tenderness in the first seconds is common in the early weeks, but pain that lasts through a feed is a sign to break suction and relatch. Pain with cracked or creased nipples, or pain that continues past the early weeks, is a reason to see a lactation consultant or your clinician, since issues like tongue-tie or infection can also play a role. How do I fix a shallow latch? To fix a shallow latch, slide a clean finger into the corner of your baby's mouth to break the suction, take them off, and start again from a wide gape with the chin touching the breast first. Line their nose up with your nipple so they tip their head back and take more of the areola below the nipple than above. If the latch keeps landing shallow after several calm tries, a hands-on session with a lactation consultant can usually find the cause quickly. What should I do if my newborn won't latch? If your newborn will not latch, calm things down first: hold them skin to skin on your bare chest and let them root, ideally before they are crying hard. Try a laid-back position, hand express a few drops of milk onto the nipple, and offer the breast at early waking signs rather than waiting for full cries. If your baby still will not latch over several feeds, contact your midwife, clinician, or a lactation consultant the same day so feeding stays on track, and call your baby's clinician right away if your baby is hard to wake or making few wet diapers.

title: Breast Milk Storage Guidelines: Room, Fridge, Freezer
description: Clear breast milk storage guidelines in one place: how long milk keeps at room temperature, in the fridge, and in the freezer, plus safe thawing, warming, and practical pumping basics.
body: Freshly expressed breast milk keeps for up to 4 hours at room temperature, up to 4 days in the refrigerator, and 6 months is best in the freezer, though up to 12 months is acceptable. These numbers come from mainstream public health guidance, including the CDC, and they apply to healthy, full-term babies at home. Keep these numbers where you can see them, then read on for thawing rules, pumping timing, and the small habits that keep a milk stash safe and usable. The storage numbers, first Here are the numbers most parents are looking for. Freshly expressed breast milk is safe at room temperature, about 25 C or 77 F, for up to 4 hours. In the refrigerator, at about 4 C or 40 F, it keeps for up to 4 days. In the freezer, 6 months is best for quality, and up to 12 months is acceptable. These times reflect mainstream public health guidance, including the CDC, and they apply to healthy, full-term babies at home. If your baby was premature or is in the hospital, the rules are stricter, so follow the times your care team gives you instead. Two more numbers matter at 3 a.m. Milk left over from a feed should be used within about 2 hours, because your baby's mouth introduces bacteria into the bottle. And milk carried in an insulated cooler with frozen ice packs is fine for up to 24 hours, which covers most workdays and travel. Storage times do not stack, so a bottle that spent 3 days in the fridge does not also get a full 4 hours on the counter. When you are not sure how long milk has been out, it is reasonable to err on the shorter side and use the freshest bottle you have. Thawing frozen milk without wasting it Thaw the oldest milk first, since quality slowly declines in the freezer. The gentlest method is to move a bag to the refrigerator the night before, which takes about 12 hours. If you need milk sooner, hold the sealed bag under lukewarm running water or set it in a bowl of warm water. Never thaw or warm breast milk in the microwave. Microwaves heat unevenly and can create hot spots that burn a baby's mouth even when the bottle feels cool on the outside. Once the ice is gone, treat the clock as started. Thawed milk follows shorter rules than fresh milk. Once fully thawed, use it within 24 hours if it stays in the refrigerator, or within 1 to 2 hours once it reaches room temperature. Never refreeze milk that has thawed. Thawed milk sometimes smells slightly soapy or metallic because of a normal enzyme called lipase; it is still safe if it was stored correctly, though some babies dislike the taste. Milk also separates in storage, with the cream rising to the top. Swirl the container gently to mix it back together instead of shaking it hard. When to start pumping, and how often If your baby is healthy and feeding well, there is usually no need to pump in the first weeks. Many lactation professionals suggest waiting until feeding feels settled, often around 3 to 4 weeks, before adding a daily pumping session to build a small freezer stash for a return to work. Starting earlier makes sense in specific situations: your baby is premature or separated from you, latching is not working yet, or a clinician has asked you to build supply. In those cases, pumping about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours mimics a newborn's feeding pattern. Milk supply works on demand and removal, so the steadier your rhythm, the steadier your output. Once you are away from your baby for feeds, try to pump roughly as often as your baby would eat, which for many families means every 3 hours or so during the workday. A session of about 15 to 20 minutes is typical, though output varies widely from person to person and even from morning to evening. Do not judge your supply by what you pump; a pump is less efficient than most babies. Questions about supply itself belong in a conversation with a lactation consultant. Label it, freeze it flat, use the oldest first Label every container with the date you expressed the milk, and add your baby's name if the milk will go to daycare. Freeze in small portions of about 2 to 4 ounces, which is 60 to 120 ml. Small portions thaw faster and waste less when your baby takes only part of a bottle. Use storage bags made for breast milk or clean food-grade containers with tight lids, and leave a little space at the top, because milk expands as it freezes. Squeeze the air out of bags and lay them flat to freeze; flat bags stack neatly and thaw quickly. Store milk at the back of the fridge or freezer, not in the door, where the temperature swings every time someone opens it. Rotate your stash so the oldest dated milk gets used first. A deep freezer held at minus 18 C, which is 0 F, gives you the full storage window; a small freezer compartment inside a fridge runs warmer, so lean toward the shorter end of the range. If keeping track feels like one job too many, jot pumping dates and amounts in the BeMama app or on a sticky note on the freezer door. A system you can follow half asleep is the right one. Warming milk and keeping everything clean Babies can drink milk cold, at room temperature, or warmed; there is no medical need to heat it. If your baby prefers warm milk, set the bottle or sealed bag in a bowl of warm water for a few minutes or use a bottle warmer. Never use a microwave, and avoid very hot water, which can damage some of the milk's protective components. Test a few drops on the inside of your wrist; it should feel comfortably warm, not hot. Once milk is warmed, use it within about 2 hours and throw away whatever is left after that. Wash pump parts that touch milk after every use with hot soapy water or in the dishwasher, and let them air dry on a clean towel. Sanitizing once daily adds a margin of safety for babies under about 2 months, premature babies, or babies with weakened immune systems. Pumping should not hurt beyond brief initial discomfort. Contact a clinician or lactation consultant for ongoing pain, cracked or bleeding nipples, a hard red painful area of the breast, or fever and chills, which can signal mastitis. Call your baby's clinician if you have concerns about weight gain or fewer wet diapers than usual. Fresh breast milk keeps up to 4 hours at room temperature, up to 4 days in the fridge, and 6 months is best in the freezer. Thawed milk must be used within 24 hours in the fridge and never refrozen. Milk left over from a feed should be used within about 2 hours. Freeze small labeled portions of 2 to 4 ounces and use the oldest milk first. Warm milk in warm water, never a microwave, and call a clinician about breast pain, fever, or feeding concerns. How long can breast milk sit out? Freshly expressed breast milk can sit out at room temperature for up to 4 hours, assuming the room is about 25 C or 77 F or cooler. Thawed milk gets less time, about 1 to 2 hours. If your baby already started drinking from the bottle, use it within about 2 hours and discard the rest. How long does breast milk last in the freezer? Breast milk keeps best for about 6 months in the freezer, and up to 12 months is acceptable. Quality slowly declines rather than the milk suddenly going bad, so use the oldest milk first. A freezer held at minus 18 C, which is 0 F, gives the most reliable storage. Can you refreeze thawed breast milk? No, once breast milk has fully thawed it should not be refrozen. Keep thawed milk in the refrigerator and use it within 24 hours, or within 1 to 2 hours once it reaches room temperature. If you often waste thawed milk, freeze smaller portions so you only thaw what your baby needs. When should I start pumping? If your baby is healthy and breastfeeding well, many families start pumping around 3 to 4 weeks, once feeding feels settled and a stash for returning to work becomes useful. Start right away, ideally within hours of birth, if your baby is premature, separated from you, or not latching yet. A lactation consultant can help you set a schedule that protects your supply.

title: How to Prepare Baby Formula Safely: Water and Mixing
description: Learn how to prepare baby formula safely: what water to use, exact mixing ratios, how long formula keeps after mixing, and simple bottle cleaning and sterilizing routines.
body: To prepare baby formula safely, wash your hands, boil fresh water and let it cool briefly so it is still at least 70 degrees Celsius, pour the measured water into a clean bottle, add level unpacked scoops exactly as the label directs, shake, then cool the bottle and test it on your wrist before feeding. Those steps exist because powdered formula is not sterile, and a few consistent habits protect young babies from rare but serious infections. This guide walks through the four moments that matter: preparing, feeding, storing, and cleaning. Why the preparation rules exist Powdered infant formula is not sterile, even when the tin is sealed and well within its date. Very rarely, powder can contain a germ called Cronobacter, which can cause serious bloodstream or brain infections in very young babies. The risk is highest for babies under about 2 months old, babies born prematurely, and babies with weakened immune systems. That is the whole reason preparation rules exist: hot enough water, exact measuring, and short standing times shrink an already small risk to something much smaller. None of this means formula is unsafe. Enormous numbers of babies are formula fed and thrive. It simply means a few habits are worth doing the same way every single time. If your baby is in one of those higher-risk groups, sterile liquid formula is the safest option, because the Cronobacter risk comes mainly from powder. Ready-to-feed bottles are sterile until you open them, and liquid concentrate is also sterile before mixing. Some families use ready-to-feed for the first weeks and switch to powder later, or keep a few bottles on hand for nights and travel. If cost makes liquid formula unrealistic, careful powder preparation with hot water, described below, is a reasonable and widely recommended approach. Talk with your pediatric team if your baby was premature or has a medical condition, since they may prefer sterile liquid for longer. Choose your water In most cities and towns, plain tap water that is safe for you to drink is also an acceptable base for formula, which is consistent with CDC guidance. If you use well water, have it tested before using it for a baby, and ask your local health department how often to retest. Bottled water is fine too, but it is not sterile, so it follows the same handling rules as tap water. If your home has older plumbing, run the cold tap briefly before filling the kettle, and always start from the cold tap rather than the hot one. If you are unsure about your supply, your baby's clinician or local public health office can advise you. For babies under about 2 months, premature babies, and babies with weakened immune systems, the WHO and the NHS advise mixing powder with water that has been boiled and then cooled for no more than about 30 minutes, so it is still at least 70 degrees Celsius, about 158 Fahrenheit. Water that hot kills Cronobacter that may be present in the powder itself. Boil fresh water, let it sit briefly, pour the measured amount into a clean bottle, then add the powder. For older, healthy babies, many families mix powder with safe room-temperature water instead. Ask your pediatrician which approach fits your baby and your situation. Measure and mix exactly as the label says Follow the ratio on your container exactly, and always put the water in the bottle first, then the powder. Use only the scoop that came in that specific container, since scoop sizes differ between brands and even between products from the same brand. Fill the scoop loosely and level it off with a clean knife; never pack it down or add a little extra for a hungrier baby. Never dilute formula to stretch a can. Extra water can cause poor growth and, in young babies, dangerous drops in blood sodium, while extra powder can strain the kidneys and cause dehydration. The printed ratio is the safe zone, so treat it like a recipe you never improvise. Cap the bottle and shake or swirl until the powder fully dissolves. If you mixed with hot water, cool the bottle quickly by holding it under cold running water or standing it in a bowl of cold water, keeping the water level below the ring so nothing splashes onto the nipple. Test a few drops on the inside of your wrist before feeding; the milk should feel warm or barely lukewarm, never hot. Do not warm any bottle in a microwave. Microwaves heat unevenly and can leave scalding pockets in milk that feels cool on the outside. A jug of warm water or a bottle warmer used as directed is the safer route. The timing rules, all in one place Once formula is mixed, a simple clock starts. Use the bottle within 2 hours of preparing it if it stays at room temperature, and within 1 hour of the moment your baby starts drinking. After a feed begins, bacteria from your baby's mouth travel back into the milk, so anything left after about an hour goes down the drain, even if it looks untouched. Do not put a partly finished bottle back in the fridge for later, and do not top it up with fresh formula. If a freshly mixed bottle has not been offered at all and less than 2 hours have passed, you can still refrigerate it promptly and use it later. Preparing ahead can save your sanity at night. Mix bottles, cool them fast, and put them straight into the back of the refrigerator, not the door; use them within 24 hours. Warm a chilled bottle once and never rewarm it. For outings, the safest options are ready-to-feed bottles or a flask of hot water plus powder measured into a clean container, mixed fresh when your baby is hungry. Tired brains lose track of timing easily, so write the mixing time on a strip of tape on each bottle, or note feed times in the BeMama app or a notebook so 2 hours never quietly becomes 5. Keep hands, bottles, and surfaces clean Clean hands and clean gear do a surprising amount of the work. Wash your hands with soap and water for about 20 seconds before preparing any bottle, and wipe down the counter you mix on. After every feed, take the bottle, nipple, and ring apart and wash them in hot soapy water with a brush kept only for baby items, or run them through the dishwasher on a hot cycle with heated drying. Rinse everything first so milk residue does not bake on. Let the pieces air dry completely on a clean rack or towel; rubbing the inside with a dish towel can add germs rather than remove them. Sanitizing goes one step beyond washing and matters most for babies under about 2 months, premature babies, and babies with weakened immune systems; the CDC suggests sanitizing at least once a day for these groups. Boil the clean parts for about 5 minutes, use a steam sterilizer as directed, or run a dishwasher sanitize cycle. Older healthy babies usually do fine with thorough washing alone. Know the escalation signs too: a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius, 100.4 Fahrenheit, or higher in a baby under 3 months is urgent, so call your clinician right away rather than waiting. Seek emergency care if your baby is unusually floppy, hard to wake, breathing with difficulty, refusing feeds, or vomiting repeatedly, since these can signal serious infection in a young baby. Powdered formula is not sterile, so careful preparation matters most in the first 2 months. For young or high-risk babies, mix powder with water still at least 70 degrees Celsius, or use sterile ready-to-feed formula. Add water first, use level unpacked scoops, and never dilute or concentrate formula. Use mixed formula within 2 hours, within 1 hour once a feed starts, and discard leftovers. Wash hands and bottle parts after every feed, sanitize daily for young babies, and never microwave a bottle. Do you need to boil water for baby formula? Yes, if your baby is under about 2 months old, premature, or has a weakened immune system: the WHO and NHS advise mixing powder with freshly boiled water cooled for no more than about 30 minutes, so it is still at least 70 degrees Celsius. That temperature kills Cronobacter that can occasionally be present in the powder itself. For older, healthy babies, safe tap or bottled water at room temperature is generally acceptable. Ask your pediatrician which approach fits your baby and your local water supply. How long is formula good after mixing? Prepared formula is good for up to 2 hours at room temperature, or up to 24 hours if you refrigerate it immediately after mixing. Once your baby starts drinking from the bottle, the window shrinks to about 1 hour. Store made-ahead bottles at the back of the fridge, not in the door, and warm each one only once. Can you reuse formula after baby drinks from the bottle? No, discard whatever is left within about 1 hour of the start of the feed. Bacteria from your baby's mouth enter the milk while drinking and can multiply, even in the refrigerator. To waste less, offer smaller amounts per bottle and mix a little more if your baby still seems hungry. How do you sterilize baby bottles? Wash the bottle parts first, then boil them for about 5 minutes, use a steam sterilizer as directed, or run a dishwasher sanitize cycle. Sanitize at least once a day for babies under about 2 months, premature babies, and babies with weakened immune systems. Let everything air dry on a clean rack rather than towel-drying the insides. Older healthy babies usually do fine with careful washing in hot soapy water after every feed.

title: How Many Wet Diapers Should a Newborn Have Each Day
description: How many wet diapers should a newborn have? A day by day counting guide from birth through the first weeks, plus what brick dust means and the dehydration signs that need a call.
body: A newborn should have roughly one wet diaper per day of life for the first several days: one on day 1, two on day 2, three on day 3, then six or more heavy wets every 24 hours from about day 5 onward. This simple count is the best home measure of whether your baby is getting enough milk. Below you will find the day by day numbers, what a real wet feels like, what brick dust means, and which changes deserve a same-day call. The day by day wet diaper count In the first days, wet diapers usually match your baby's day of life. Expect at least one wet diaper in the first 24 hours, at least two on day 2, three on day 3, and four on day 4. The count climbs each day because colostrum comes in small amounts and your baby's stomach is tiny at first. Around day 4 or 5, as milk volume increases, output rises quickly. From about day 5 onward, most well-fed newborns produce six or more noticeably heavy wet diapers every 24 hours, and that pace continues for months. This is the same counting guide most hospitals teach at discharge, so it should match what your nurse or midwife told you. Count in 24-hour blocks starting from the time of birth, not from midnight, at least for the first week. A simple tally works: mark every diaper that contains clear or pale urine, even if it also contains stool. Small pees still count in the first two or three days, because a baby drinking colostrum produces very little urine. If you are too tired to remember, jot the time of each change on paper or in the BeMama app so you can answer the nurse's questions at the first checkup. Formula-fed babies often reach six wets slightly sooner because they usually take larger volumes from the first day, but the same day-of-life guide applies to them too. Why wet diapers are the best home measure of intake Wet diapers matter because you cannot see how much milk goes into a breastfed baby. There is no bottle to measure, weight checks happen at the clinic rather than at home, and newborns feed in short, sleepy bursts that are hard to judge. Urine output is the practical stand-in: fluid that goes in must come out. When a baby is getting enough milk, the kidneys make plenty of pale urine and the diaper count rises on schedule. When intake falls short, urine becomes scant, dark, and strong smelling well before other signs appear. That is why every early pediatric visit starts with the same question: how many wet diapers in the last 24 hours? Treat the count as a screening tool, not a verdict. It works best alongside two other home signals: feeding frequency and behavior. Most newborns feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours in the early weeks, and you should hear or see swallowing during feeds. A baby who feeds often, swallows audibly, seems satisfied for a stretch afterward, and produces wets on schedule is usually doing well. Stool patterns add information too, and they are covered in our separate newborn poop guide. The confirming measure is weight, checked at your baby's early appointments. If the diaper count looks fine but feeding feels wrong to you, ask for a weight check anyway. Your instinct is data. What a wet diaper actually feels like Modern disposable diapers absorb so well that a real wet can be easy to miss. Here is a concrete benchmark: pour 3 tablespoons, about 45 milliliters, of water into a clean, dry diaper. Pick it up and feel the weight. That is roughly what one reasonable wet diaper feels like once your milk has come in. When you are unsure about a used diaper, compare it against a fresh one in the other hand. Many disposables also have a wetness indicator, a line that turns from yellow to blue when urine touches it, though a very small pee may not change the whole line. If you use cloth, wetness is usually much easier to feel directly. Expect the feel of the diaper to change across the first week. On days 1 to 3, wets are small and light because colostrum comes in teaspoon-sized amounts, and that is normal. From about day 5, diapers should start to feel noticeably heavy, close to the 3-tablespoon benchmark or beyond it. Urine color is a second clue: pale yellow with a mild smell is reassuring, while dark yellow, strong-smelling urine in small amounts suggests your baby needs more milk. If you cannot tell whether a diaper is wet at all, tuck a tissue or a cotton pad inside at one change. It will show even a small pee clearly. Brick dust and urate crystals Brick dust is the name for a pink, orange, or rust-colored powdery stain in the diaper. It comes from urate crystals, a normal byproduct that appears when a newborn's urine is concentrated. It is common on days 1 to 3, while milk is still coming in and babies are drinking small volumes. Despite the alarming color, brick dust is not blood, and on its own in the first few days it does not mean something is wrong. It usually appears exactly where the urine landed, as a dry, chalky patch rather than a wet red streak. Take a photo if you want to show it to the clinician later. Timing is what matters. If brick dust keeps appearing past about day 4, or shows up alongside fewer wet diapers than expected, call your baby's clinician or lactation support the same day. Persistent crystals usually mean the baby needs more milk, and feeding can often be adjusted quickly once someone watches a feed. Anything that looks truly red and wet, like fresh blood, deserves a call whenever it appears. One exception worth knowing: baby girls can have a small amount of vaginal spotting in the first week from hormone withdrawal after birth, and that is expected. When you are not sure what you are seeing, ask. These are routine questions for newborn clinics. Dehydration signs and when to call Dehydration in a newborn usually shows in the diaper first. Watch for fewer wet diapers than your baby's day of age during the first week, fewer than six wets per 24 hours after day 5, or a long dry stretch, for example no urine for 6 to 8 hours. Dark, strong-smelling urine and returning brick dust are earlier hints. Beyond the diaper, look for a dry mouth and lips, a sunken soft spot on the head, unusual sleepiness, difficulty waking your baby to feed, or feeds that keep getting shorter and weaker. Newborns have small reserves, so these signs deserve a same-day call rather than a wait-and-see approach. Call your baby's clinician the same day if the count drops below the day-of-life guide, and seek care urgently if your baby will not wake to feed, has a sunken soft spot, or has produced no urine in more than 8 hours. Bring your tally: the number of wets, the number of feeds, and when each happened. Concrete numbers help the clinic decide quickly whether you need a visit, a weight check, or a simple feeding adjustment. Nobody will think you overreacted. Newborn clinics expect these calls in the first two weeks, and output questions are exactly what they are staffed to answer. Expect roughly one wet diaper per day of life for the first four to five days. From about day 5, look for six or more heavy wet diapers every 24 hours. A reasonable wet feels like 3 tablespoons of water poured into a dry diaper. Brick dust is common in the first few days but worth a call if it persists past about day 4. Call the same day for fewer wets than expected, dark urine, a dry mouth, a sunken soft spot, or unusual sleepiness. How many wet diapers should a newborn have? Roughly one wet diaper per day of life for the first several days, then six or more per 24 hours from about day 5 onward. That means one wet on day 1, two on day 2, and so on until milk volume increases. After the first week, six to eight heavy wets a day is a typical, reassuring pattern. How many wet diapers should my baby have on day 3? About three wet diapers in the 24 hours of day 3. Counts a little above that are fine, and small pees still count while your baby is drinking colostrum. If your baby has fewer than three, or the urine is dark or leaves brick dust stains, contact your baby's clinician or feeding support that day. Is brick dust in a newborn diaper normal? Yes, in the first few days it is usually normal. The pink-orange stain comes from urate crystals in concentrated urine, which is common while milk is coming in. If it keeps appearing past about day 4, or comes with fewer wet diapers than expected, call your baby's clinician, because it can mean your baby needs more milk. What are the signs of dehydration in a newborn? The main signs are fewer wet diapers than expected for your baby's age, dark strong-smelling urine, a dry mouth, a sunken soft spot, and unusual sleepiness or weak feeding. In the first week, fewer wets than your baby's day of life is the clearest flag. These signs deserve a same-day call, and a baby who will not wake to feed or has had no urine in more than 8 hours needs urgent care.

title: Newborn Poop Colors: What Is Normal and What Is Not
description: A calm newborn poop color guide: the normal timeline from meconium to yellow or tan stools, how often babies go, and which colors need a same-day call to your clinician.
body: Normal newborn poop color follows a predictable path: black and tarry meconium in the first 1 to 2 days, greenish brown around days 3 to 4, then yellow and seedy or tan and pasty by about day 5. After that, almost any shade of yellow, green, or brown is fine. The colors that need a same-day call are white or chalky pale, red, and black that returns after the first week. This guide walks through the timeline, the wide normal range, and the few changes worth checking. The first week, diaper by diaper The first stools are meconium: black or very dark green, thick, sticky, and tar-like. Meconium is made of everything your baby swallowed before birth, and most babies pass it within the first 24 to 48 hours. It can cling to skin like glue, so a thin layer of barrier cream at each change makes wiping easier. If your baby has not passed any stool by 48 hours of age, tell your care team, because they will want to check that everything is moving through as it should. In a hospital or birth center, this is usually tracked for you. Around days 3 to 4, stools usually turn greenish brown and looser. These transitional stools mean milk is moving through and meconium is clearing. By about day 5, most breastfed babies pass yellow, loose stools with small seedy flecks, and many go 3 to 4 times a day or more. Formula-fed babies tend toward tan or yellow-brown paste, often a little firmer and sometimes less frequent. The exact day each stage arrives varies, especially while feeding is getting established. A rough rule: by the end of the first week, stool should no longer be black. Yellow, green, and brown are almost always fine Once meconium has cleared, almost any shade of yellow, green, or brown counts as normal. Mustard yellow, bright yellow, olive, khaki, brown with green streaks: all fine. Color can shift from one diaper to the next without meaning anything, because stool color mostly reflects how fast milk moved through the gut and how much bile pigment came along for the ride. Faster transit tends to look greener, slower transit browner. Neither is a problem on its own. If your baby is feeding, settling, and producing stools somewhere in this color family, the diaper is doing its job. Green stool in a breastfed baby is common and usually harmless, particularly when the baby is gaining weight and content between feeds. Everyday causes include a fast letdown, a recent growth spurt, something in your own diet, or an iron-fortified vitamin or formula top-up. Occasional frothy green stools sometimes follow feeds that were heavy on the first, thinner milk, which can happen when feeds are short or sides are switched quickly. If green stools come with poor weight gain, blood, lots of mucus, or a very unsettled baby, mention it to your clinician rather than reorganizing feeding on your own. White, red, and black: the colors that need a call Three colors are worth a same-day call to your baby's clinician. White, gray, or chalky pale stool can mean bile is not reaching the gut, which needs prompt assessment; it sometimes travels with jaundice, which our jaundice guide covers. Red blood, whether streaks or clots, should always be checked, even though the common causes in newborns are often minor, such as a small anal fissure or blood swallowed from cracked nipples during feeds. Black, tarry stool that comes back after meconium has fully cleared can indicate digested blood and also deserves a same-day conversation. Before you call, keep the diaper or take a clear photo in good light, because colors are hard to describe from memory at 2 a.m. Note when the color started, how your baby is feeding, and whether anything else has changed. Two look-alikes are worth knowing about: iron drops or iron-fortified formula can darken stool, and in the first few days, pinkish orange urate crystals in urine can leave a brick-dust stain on the diaper that gets mistaken for blood. Let the clinician decide whether it is a look-alike. Seek urgent care right away if unusual stool comes with a baby who is hard to wake, refusing feeds, vomiting green, or has a swollen, tender belly. How often newborns poop, and when less is fine In the first week, stool frequency usually climbs day by day, and by around day 5 many babies pass 3 to 4 stools a day or more. Some breastfed babies go after nearly every feed, which is normal and not diarrhea. Frequency in the early days is one useful sign that feeding is going well, so if your baby is passing very few stools in the first week, bring it up with your midwife, nurse, or pediatric clinician along with how feeding is going. They will look at the whole picture, including weight, rather than the diaper count alone. After the first several weeks, the range widens dramatically. Some breastfed babies shift to one stool every few days, occasionally longer, and that can be normal as long as the stool stays soft, the baby feeds well, and the belly stays soft and comfortable. Formula-fed babies usually keep a more regular daily rhythm. Grunting, straining, and going red in the face are normal newborn mechanics, not constipation. True constipation in a young baby means hard, dry, pellet-like stools, and it is uncommon; it deserves a clinician's input rather than home remedies. Wet diapers are a separate story, and our diaper output guide covers those counts. Texture, mucus, and keeping track without obsessing Normal newborn stool is loose. Breastfed stool often looks like mustard with sesame seeds, and formula stool like smooth peanut butter or hummus. A little stringy mucus now and then is usually nothing, often just fast transit or swallowed mucus during a stuffy spell; frequent mucus, or mucus together with blood, is worth a call. Watery stool that soaks straight into the diaper at every change can mean diarrhea, and young babies can get dehydrated quickly, so call the same day; if there is also a fever or your baby will not feed, seek care right away. Smell changes too, from almost sweet in breastfed babies to noticeably stronger with formula. You do not need a spreadsheet of every diaper forever. In the first week or two, a simple tally of stools and their color helps you and your care team confirm feeding is on track. After that, most parents only need to note the unusual: a new color, blood, mucus, or a big change in pattern. Jotting the date and a quick description in the BeMama app, or on paper, saves you from reconstructing the whole week from memory at a checkup. And when in doubt, bring the photo. Clinicians look at stool pictures all the time, and yours will not be the strangest. Meconium is black and tarry and usually passes within the first 24 to 48 hours. By about day 5, expect yellow seedy stools with breastfeeding or tan paste with formula. After meconium clears, yellow, green, and brown stools are almost always normal. White or chalky pale stool, red blood, or returning black stool needs a same-day call. Stool frequency varies widely after the early weeks, especially in breastfed babies. What should newborn poop look like? By the end of the first week, newborn poop is usually mustard yellow and seedy in breastfed babies, or tan and paste-like in formula-fed babies. Before that, expect black tarry meconium for the first 1 to 2 days and greenish brown transitional stools around days 3 to 4. Loose textures are normal at this age and do not mean diarrhea on their own. How often should a newborn poop? By around day 5, many newborns pass 3 to 4 stools a day or more, and some breastfed babies go after nearly every feed. Very few stools in the first week is worth mentioning to your care team, because early stool output partly reflects how feeding is going. After the first several weeks the range widens, and some breastfed babies normally go a few days between soft stools. Why is my breastfed baby's poop green? Green poop in a breastfed baby is common and usually harmless, especially when your baby is feeding well and gaining weight. Fast milk flow, growth spurts, something in your own diet, and iron supplements can all shift stool toward green. Check with your clinician if green stools come with blood, lots of mucus, poor weight gain, or a very unsettled baby. What does blood in newborn stool mean? Blood in newborn stool should be checked by a clinician the same day, even though the common causes are often minor. Small streaks can come from a tiny anal fissure or from blood swallowed during feeds when nipples are cracked. Keep the diaper or take a photo, and seek urgent care if blood comes with vomiting, fever, a swollen belly, or a baby who seems unwell.

title: Newborn Jaundice: Causes, Timeline, and Treatment
description: What newborn jaundice is, when it usually appears and fades, how bilirubin is checked, how feeding and phototherapy help, and the warning signs that need a prompt call.
body: Newborn jaundice is a yellow tint in a baby's skin and eyes caused by bilirubin, a normal byproduct of red blood cells that a newborn's liver is still learning to clear. It is very common, usually appears around days 2 to 4 of life, and typically fades within about 2 weeks. Most cases need nothing more than good feeding and a scheduled check. The main exception is yellowing in the first 24 hours, which always needs prompt medical attention. What bilirubin is and why newborns turn yellow Every day, your body breaks down old red blood cells. One of the leftovers is bilirubin, a yellow pigment. In healthy adults, the liver processes bilirubin quickly and it leaves the body in stool, so it never builds up enough to see. A newborn is different in two ways. Babies are born with extra red blood cells that break down quickly after birth, so more bilirubin is produced. At the same time, a newborn's liver is immature and clears bilirubin slowly for the first days of life. When bilirubin builds up faster than it leaves, it settles in the skin and the whites of the eyes and gives them a yellow tint. That tint is jaundice. This ordinary version is called physiologic jaundice, and it is extremely common. Most newborns develop at least some visible yellowing in the first week, and premature babies are even more likely to. In the large majority of cases the level stays low, the liver catches up, and the color fades on its own. Jaundice becomes a medical problem only when bilirubin climbs unusually high or rises unusually fast, which is why your baby's care team checks it rather than guessing by eye. Knowing that the yellow tint has a boring explanation helps: for most families, jaundice is something to watch and feed through, not something to fear. The usual timeline, and the one bright line In healthy full-term babies, jaundice typically appears around days 2 to 4 of life, peaks around days 3 to 5, and fades within about 2 weeks. Premature babies often peak a little later and can take closer to 3 weeks to clear. The yellow color usually starts in the face and the whites of the eyes, then moves down the chest and belly as the level rises, and fades in the reverse order. You do not need to track this hour by hour. What matters is the general pattern: appearing after the first full day, drifting up for a few days, then steadily improving while your baby feeds well and wakes normally. There is one bright line every parent should know: jaundice that is visible in the first 24 hours of life is never considered routine. Early yellowing can signal that red blood cells are breaking down faster than normal, for example from a blood group mismatch between you and your baby, and pediatric guidance treats it as a reason for prompt testing rather than watchful waiting. If you notice a yellow tint on the first day, in the hospital or at home, tell a nurse or call your baby's clinician right away. Most of these babies do well, precisely because early checking allows early treatment. How jaundice is actually checked At home, the classic check is simple: in good natural light, press gently on your baby's nose or forehead for a second, then let go. Skin that looks yellow where you pressed suggests jaundice. Also glance at the whites of the eyes and the gums. Be aware that checking by eye is less reliable on darker skin tones, where yellowing may show mainly in the eyes and gums, so do not rely on skin color alone if something feels off. Checking once or twice a day in the first week is plenty. If the yellow seems to be spreading down past the belly to the arms or legs, that is a reason to call, not just watch. Clinicians do not guess by eye either. Most hospitals measure every baby's bilirubin before discharge, using a painless skin sensor called a transcutaneous meter or a small heel-prick blood sample. The result is plotted against your baby's age in hours, which tells the team whether the level is expected or rising too fast. That is also why the first follow-up visit, usually within a day or two of going home, matters so much: it catches the peak days. Keep the appointment even if your baby looks fine to you. It can help to note the discharge bilirubin result and the follow-up date somewhere easy to find, such as the BeMama app or the discharge folder. Feeding helps, and what phototherapy really involves Bilirubin leaves the body mainly through stool, so the everyday treatment for mild jaundice is frequent, effective feeding. For breastfed newborns that usually means 8 to 12 feeds in 24 hours in the early weeks, while formula-fed babies typically feed about every 3 to 4 hours. More milk in means more stool out, and more stool out means bilirubin leaving faster. If feeding is not going smoothly, ask for help with latch and feeding cues early, because a sleepy jaundiced baby can slip into a cycle of feeding less and clearing less. Extra water is not recommended: it does not lower bilirubin and can displace milk. Any decision about supplementing belongs with your baby's clinician. If bilirubin crosses the treatment threshold for your baby's age, the standard treatment is phototherapy. It looks more dramatic than it is. Your baby lies in a bassinet under blue light, wearing only a diaper and soft eye shields, or is wrapped in a fiberoptic blanket. The light changes bilirubin in the skin into a form the body can pass in urine and stool without the liver's help. It is not ultraviolet light, it does not hurt, and babies come out for feeds and cuddles on a schedule the team sets. Many babies need it for only a day or two. Putting a baby in direct sunlight is not a safe substitute and is not recommended. Breastfeeding patterns and the call-now signs Two breastfeeding-related patterns are worth telling apart. In the first week, jaundice sometimes rises because a baby is not yet getting enough milk, often while supply is still building. This is sometimes called suboptimal intake jaundice, and the fix is more effective feeding, not stopping breastfeeding. Separately, some thriving breastfed babies stay mildly yellow for 3 to 12 weeks. This is called breast milk jaundice, it is generally harmless, and breastfeeding continues, but the label belongs to a clinician who has confirmed the baby is gaining weight and ruled out other causes. One pointer worth remembering: jaundice that comes with pale, chalky stools or dark urine always needs a medical review. Call your baby's clinician promptly if the yellow color is deepening or spreading below the belly to the arms and legs, if your baby is feeding poorly, unusually hard to wake, or limp, or if jaundice appears in the first 24 hours or is still obvious after 2 weeks. Seek emergency care right away for a high-pitched cry, arching of the neck or back, a fever, or a baby who will not wake to feed. These signs are rare, and the reason to know them is reassurance: very high bilirubin is treatable when caught, and modern checking makes serious harm uncommon. When in doubt, call. Jaundice questions are a routine part of newborn care, and no one will think you overreacted. Most newborn jaundice appears around days 2 to 4 and fades within about 2 weeks. Yellowing in the first 24 hours of life always needs prompt medical evaluation. Bilirubin is checked with a painless skin meter or a small blood test, not by eye alone. Frequent, effective feeding helps babies clear bilirubin faster. Call your clinician for deepening yellow, poor feeding, or extreme sleepiness; a high-pitched cry or arching needs emergency care. When does newborn jaundice go away? In most healthy full-term babies, newborn jaundice fades within about 2 weeks, after peaking around days 3 to 5. Premature babies can take closer to 3 weeks. Some thriving breastfed babies stay mildly yellow for 3 to 12 weeks with breast milk jaundice, which a clinician should confirm. Jaundice that is still obvious after 2 weeks deserves a check even if your baby seems well. Is jaundice in newborns dangerous? Usually not: most newborn jaundice is mild, harmless, and fades on its own as the liver matures. It becomes a concern only when bilirubin rises very high or very fast, which, if untreated, can rarely injure the brain. That risk is exactly what routine bilirubin checks and phototherapy are designed to prevent. Jaundice in the first 24 hours, deepening color, poor feeding, or extreme sleepiness are the signs that need prompt attention. How can I tell if my baby has jaundice? Press gently on your baby's nose or forehead in good natural light, then let go: if the skin looks yellow where you pressed, your baby likely has some jaundice. Check the whites of the eyes and the gums too, especially on darker skin tones where skin color is harder to judge. If you are unsure, ask for a bilirubin check, which uses a painless skin meter or a small blood sample. Does breastfeeding help jaundice? Yes, frequent and effective breastfeeding helps clear jaundice, because milk drives the stools that carry bilirubin out of the body. Aim for 8 to 12 feeds in 24 hours in the early weeks, and ask for feeding help early if latching is hard. Jaundice is rarely a reason to stop breastfeeding, even in longer-lasting breast milk jaundice. Your baby's clinician can advise if supplementing is ever needed.

title: Newborn Fever: Why 100.4 F Means Call Right Away
description: A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher is a newborn fever that needs same day medical care. What to do, how to measure, and what to avoid.
body: A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher in a baby under 3 months old is a fever, and it means calling a clinician right away, even at night, so your baby is evaluated the same day. In a baby under 28 days, treat it as an emergency and seek care right away. Young infants can have serious infections with almost no other signs, so the number alone is the reason to call. This guide covers how to measure accurately, what to do next, and why unusually low readings matter too. Why 100.4 F is the line for young babies For a baby under 3 months old, a rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher is a fever, and at this age it is never something to watch and wait on. Pediatric guidance, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, advises that these babies be evaluated by a clinician the same day, and a baby under 28 days should be seen urgently, usually in an emergency department. This is true even if your baby is feeding, sleeping, and acting normally. The number itself is the signal. You are not overreacting by calling at 2 a.m., and no reasonable clinician will think you are. The reason for the strict cutoff is how young immune systems work. In the first weeks of life, a baby's defenses are still immature, and bacteria can spread quickly through the blood, urine, or spinal fluid without producing the obvious signs an older child would show. A newborn with a serious infection may look only slightly off, or may look fine. Fever is sometimes the single clue, which is why clinicians take one reading so seriously. Once a baby is past 3 months, the rules relax and behavior starts to matter more than the number. Before then, the threshold does the deciding for you. How to take your newborn's temperature A rectal reading with a digital thermometer is the standard at this age because it reflects core temperature most accurately. Wash the thermometer tip with soap and cool water, then coat it with a little petroleum jelly or a water-based lubricant. Lay your baby on their back and lift the legs gently toward the chest, or place them belly down across your lap. Insert the tip about half an inch, no more than one inch, and stop if you feel resistance. Hold it still until it beeps, then read the number and write it down with the time. Label that thermometer rectal only so it never gets used for mouths. Forehead and armpit thermometers are useful for screening, but they can read high or low, so they should not make the final call at this age. If a forehead or armpit reading looks raised, or your baby simply feels hot to you, confirm with a rectal measurement before deciding anything. If you cannot take a rectal reading, call the clinician anyway and say which method you used. Ear thermometers are not reliable in young babies because the ear canal is too small. Do not add or subtract a degree to convert one method to another; just take a rectal reading. And skip the wrist-on-forehead test as your only check. Hands are good at noticing warmth and bad at measuring it. What to do when the number is 100.4 F or higher Call your baby's clinician or nurse line right away, whatever the hour. If your baby is under 28 days old, go to an emergency department; most clinicians will send you there anyway, because babies this young usually need tests such as urine and blood work to rule out serious infection. If your baby is between 28 days and 3 months, the clinician will tell you whether to come to the office quickly or go straight to emergency care. Do not wait to see whether the fever comes down on its own, and do not wait for morning. A fever that fades for a few hours can still mean infection. Before you leave, or while you wait for a callback, note the exact reading, the time, and how you measured it, in the BeMama app or on paper. If you took more than one reading, note them all. This small record genuinely helps, because the care team will ask when the fever started and how high it went. Dress your baby in a normal single layer for the trip, not extra bundling. Bring the thermometer if it is easy to grab. Feeding can continue as usual unless a clinician says otherwise. Your only jobs right now are to get seen and to keep the timeline straight. What not to do before your baby is seen Do not give acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen unless a clinician specifically directs it. Fever medicine is not dangerous in the right dose, but at this age the dose must come from a professional, and lowering the number before evaluation hides the very information the team needs. Ibuprofen is not used in babies under about 6 months at all. If a clinician does recommend acetaminophen, they will give you a dose based on your baby's weight; never guess from the package, which does not cover young infants. A fever brought down at home is still a fever that happened, and it still needs the same evaluation. Do not assume warm clothing explains the reading without proving it. If your baby was heavily bundled or in a hot room, undress them to a single light layer, wait about 15 to 30 minutes, and take another rectal reading. If it is still 100.4 F or higher, call. If it has dropped below the line, keep the room comfortable, recheck later, and call anyway if anything about your baby worries you. Skip cold baths, cool sponging, and rubbing alcohol; they can cause shivering or harm and do not treat the cause. Rechecking every ten minutes all night is not a plan either. One confirmed reading is enough to act on. A low temperature needs a call too Fever is not the only reading that matters in a newborn. A rectal temperature below about 97.5 F (36.4 C) also deserves a prompt call to your baby's clinician. Young babies lose heat quickly and are not yet good at holding a steady temperature, so a low number sometimes just means a cool room or damp clothes. But in newborns, a low temperature can also be a sign of infection, in the same way a fever can. Clinicians treat an unusually low reading in a young infant with the same seriousness as a high one, which is why it earns a call rather than a shrug. If the reading is low, warm your baby the simple way: dry clothes, a hat, skin to skin contact against your chest with a blanket over both of you, and a comfortably warm room. Recheck after about 30 minutes. If the temperature stays below 97.5 F despite warming, or your baby is hard to wake or feeding poorly, seek medical care promptly rather than continuing to warm and wait. Avoid hot water bottles, heating pads, and space heaters aimed at the crib; they can overheat or burn a newborn quickly. As with fever, you are not measuring to reassure yourself. You are measuring to know when to call. A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher in a baby under 3 months needs same day medical care. For a baby under 28 days, go to emergency care right away. Rectal measurement is the standard at this age; forehead and armpit readings are screening only. Do not give fever medicine before evaluation unless a clinician tells you to. A rectal reading below about 97.5 F (36.4 C) also deserves a prompt call. What temperature is a fever for a newborn? A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher is a fever in a newborn. In any baby under 3 months, that number means same day medical evaluation, even if your baby seems well. Forehead and armpit readings are screening only, so confirm with a rectal measurement before deciding anything. Is 100.4 a fever for a baby? Yes. A rectal reading of 100.4 F (38.0 C) is the fever threshold for babies, and under 3 months it is the level at which clinicians want the baby seen the same day. It is a call now number, not a watch and wait number, because young infants can have serious infections with few other signs. Can you give Tylenol to a newborn? Not unless a clinician directs it. Acetaminophen dosing in babies under 12 weeks should come from a professional and be based on your baby's weight, and giving it before an evaluation can hide the fever the care team needs to see. Ibuprofen is not used under about 6 months. Call first; if medicine is appropriate, you will get an exact dose. When should I take my baby to the ER for a fever? Go to the emergency department for any rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher in a baby under 28 days old. For a baby between 28 days and 3 months, call your clinician immediately; depending on the hour and your baby's history, they may see you urgently or send you to emergency care. If you cannot reach anyone, go to the ER rather than waiting.

title: Safe Sleep for Newborns: The ABCs and Room Sharing
description: Safe sleep for newborns comes down to the ABCs and room sharing: baby alone, on their back, in a bare crib, in your room for at least six months.
body: Safe sleep for newborns comes down to the ABCs: your baby sleeps Alone, on their Back, in a bare Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat mattress, in your room but not in your bed. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends room sharing for at least the first six months, because it lowers the risk of sudden infant death while keeping night feeds manageable. This guide walks through each rule, what your baby can and cannot sleep in, and what to do when you are too tired to trust yourself at 2 a.m. The ABCs: alone, on the back, in a bare crib Safe sleep has three rules, often called the ABCs. Alone: your baby sleeps in their own space, not in an adult bed, and not sharing a surface with a parent, sibling, or pet. Back: you place your baby on their back for every sleep, at night and for every nap, until their first birthday. Crib: the space is a crib, bassinet, or play yard with a firm, flat, non-inclined mattress and a fitted sheet, and nothing else inside. No pillow, no blanket, no soft toy. These three rules come from decades of research into sudden infant death syndrome, and they are the same rules hospitals follow in the nursery. The rules matter most in the first six months, when the risk of sleep-related death is highest, and they apply to every sleep, not just the ones at home. A nap at grandma's house counts. A stroller doze that turns into a long sleep counts. Anyone who cares for your baby, including grandparents, babysitters, and daycare staff, should hear the same instructions from you, because older relatives often learned different advice. If a claim sounds like a shortcut, such as a product that promises safe bed sharing, treat it with suspicion. Nothing on the market changes the basics: alone, on the back, in a bare crib. Room sharing: same room, separate surface The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that your baby sleep in your room, close to your bed but on their own separate surface, ideally for at least the first six months. Room sharing is linked to a lower risk of SIDS, and it makes the nights easier in practical ways. You can hear your baby, respond quickly, feed, and settle them again without walking down a hall. A bassinet or crib within arm's reach of your side of the bed works well. If your bedroom is small, a compact play yard that meets current safety standards does the same job. The room does not need to be silent or dark to be safe. Bed sharing is different, and it raises risk rather than lowering it. Adult mattresses are softer than crib mattresses, and adult beds hold pillows, duvets, and gaps between the mattress and headboard or wall where a baby can become trapped. The risk of bed sharing is higher when a baby is under about four months old, was born early or small, or when a parent smokes, has had alcohol, has taken any sedating medicine, or is severely sleep deprived, which describes many new parents at some point. Room sharing gives you most of the closeness with far less of the risk. Same room, separate surface is the balance the evidence supports. What a baby can sleep in, and what to leave out A safe sleep space is a crib, bassinet, or portable play yard that meets current safety standards, with a firm, flat, non-inclined mattress and a fitted sheet made for that mattress. Firm means the surface springs back and does not hug your baby's head. Flat means no wedge, no incline, and no propping up the mattress after a stuffy night. If you use a second-hand crib, check that it has not been recalled, that no hardware is missing, and that it is not an older drop-side model. Your baby does not need anything else in the space. A bare bed can look sparse to adult eyes, and that is exactly what safe looks like. Keep these out of the sleep space: pillows, blankets, quilts, bumper pads, stuffed animals, sleep positioners, weighted sleepers, and weighted swaddles. Skip inclined sleepers entirely; several have been recalled, and an inclined surface can let a baby's head fall forward and block the airway. Car seats, swings, and bouncers are not sleep spaces either. They are fine for travel or short supervised awake time, but a baby who falls asleep in one should be moved to a firm, flat surface as soon as it is practical. If your baby will only nap in motion for a stretch, you are not failing; just keep working back toward the flat surface for routine sleep. Back sleeping, for every sleep and every nap Babies sleep on their backs because back sleeping keeps the airway in the safest position and is linked to a much lower risk of sudden infant death. Many parents worry that a baby on their back will choke on spit-up. Healthy babies have reflexes that make them swallow or cough up fluid, and the anatomy of the airway protects a back-sleeping baby better than a stomach-sleeping one. If your baby ever turns blue or gray, goes limp, or stops breathing, call 911 right away; that is an emergency, not a sleep position question. Side sleeping is not a safe compromise, because a baby on their side can roll to the stomach. Place your baby on their back for every sleep from the very first night, and ask anyone else who puts your baby down to do the same. Once your baby can roll from back to stomach and from stomach to back on their own, usually somewhere in the middle of the first year, you can leave them in the position they choose, though you should still lay them down on their back to start. Rolling is also a good prompt to recheck the sleep space, because a mobile baby can reach things near the crib rail that a newborn never could. Talk with your baby's clinician before changing anything for a medical reason. True medical exceptions to back sleeping are rare, and if one applies to your baby, it should come from the care team in clear written instructions, not from a forum or a relative's memory. The 2 a.m. version of the rules Following every rule is easy at 10 a.m. and much harder during a night feed when your eyes will not stay open. Plan for that version of yourself. If there is any chance you will fall asleep while feeding, feed in your adult bed with pillows, blankets, and duvets moved away, rather than on a sofa or armchair. Falling asleep with a baby on a couch or cushioned chair is far more dangerous than falling asleep in a prepared bed. The moment you wake, move your baby back to their own sleep space. This is not permission to bed share; it is a backup plan for a risk every exhausted parent faces. A few habits add protection on top of the ABCs. Offering a pacifier at the start of sleep is associated with lower SIDS risk; if it falls out after your baby drifts off, you do not need to put it back. Keep your home and car smoke free, since smoke exposure raises risk. Breastfeeding, when it is possible for your family, is also protective. Avoid overheating: skip hats indoors, and check the back of your baby's neck or their chest during sleep; sweating or hot skin means they are too warm. If questions come up at 2 a.m., note them in BeMama or on paper and bring them to the next checkup instead of settling for a midnight search result. Place your baby on their back for every sleep and every nap until age one. Use a bare crib, bassinet, or play yard with a firm, flat, non-inclined mattress. Share a room, not a bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Keep out pillows, blankets, bumpers, positioners, and weighted or inclined products. If you might doze during a feed, a prepared adult bed is safer than a sofa. How long should baby sleep in your room? At least the first 6 months, ideally: the AAP recommends that your baby sleep in your room, close to your bed but on their own separate surface, for that long or longer. Room sharing is linked to a lower risk of SIDS and makes night feeds easier. There is no hard deadline to move them out; many families transition sometime after six months when everyone's sleep starts to suffer. Why do babies have to sleep on their backs? Back sleeping is linked to a much lower risk of sudden infant death syndrome, which is why it is recommended for every sleep until the first birthday. Healthy babies do not choke more on their backs; their airway anatomy and reflexes protect them in that position. If your baby often chokes, gags, or seems to pause in breathing, contact your clinician rather than changing sleep position on your own. When can baby sleep with a blanket? Not before 12 months: current guidance is to keep blankets, pillows, and all soft bedding out of the sleep space for at least the first year. Until then, use a wearable blanket or sleep sack for warmth. After the first birthday, a small, light blanket becomes a reasonable option for most toddlers. Is it safe to co sleep with a newborn? Sharing a bed with a newborn is not recommended, because bed sharing raises the risk of sudden infant death and suffocation. Sharing a room is different: it is recommended and protective. If there is a real chance you will fall asleep during a feed, feed in a bed cleared of pillows and blankets rather than on a sofa, and move your baby back to their own space when you wake.

title: How to Swaddle a Baby Safely and When to Stop
description: A calm, step by step guide to how to swaddle a baby safely: the right tightness, hip healthy wrapping, night sleep rules, and when to stop swaddling.
body: To swaddle a baby safely, wrap a thin blanket snugly around the arms and chest, keep the wrap loose around the hips and knees, leave the face fully uncovered, and always place your baby on their back to sleep. Done that way, swaddling is considered acceptable by mainstream pediatric guidance, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, and it helps many newborns settle. It also comes with an end date: you stop at the very first sign your baby is trying to roll, often by around 2 months. Why swaddling calms newborns Newborns spend nine months held snugly on all sides, so the wide open feeling of a crib can be startling. A good swaddle recreates some of that gentle, even pressure. It also softens the startle reflex, the sudden arm fling that jolts many young babies awake just as they drift off. For lots of newborns, that combination means easier settling, longer stretches of calm, and less frantic crying in the first weeks. Not every baby agrees. Some squirm, grunt, and fight the wrap from day one, and that is normal too. Swaddling is one soothing option among several, not a requirement for good sleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics considers swaddling acceptable when it is done correctly: baby on the back for every sleep, the wrap snug at the chest but loose at the hips, and a firm plan to stop as soon as rolling attempts begin. It helps to think of swaddling as a comfort tool rather than a safety device. A swaddle does not make sleep safer on its own, and a poorly done one can add risk. If your baby consistently hates being wrapped, you lose nothing by skipping it. Feeding, rocking, white noise, and skin to skin contact can do similar calming work. How to swaddle, step by step Lay a thin blanket on a flat surface like a diamond and fold the top corner down about a hand's width. Place your baby on their back with the shoulders just below the fold. Gently straighten the left arm at the side or bend it across the chest, then bring the left side of the blanket over that arm and the chest and tuck it under the right side of the back. Fold the bottom corner up loosely over the feet, leaving plenty of room for the legs. Finally, do the same with the right arm, bring the remaining side of the blanket across the chest, and tuck it under the left side. The face and head must stay completely uncovered, with the fabric no higher than the shoulders. The right tightness has a simple test: the wrap should be snug enough across the arms and chest that it cannot work loose during sleep, yet you should still be able to slide two to three fingers flat between the fabric and your baby's chest. Loose fabric near the face is the bigger danger, so err on the side of a secure chest wrap and a roomy bottom. Arms can go in or out. Arms wrapped down or across the chest calm the startle reflex best for most newborns, while wrapping under the armpits with arms free works well for babies who fight the wrap or who are getting close to the transition out. Keep the hips loose A swaddle that presses the legs straight down and together puts steady pressure on hip joints that are still soft and forming.
