Co-viewing turns screens into conversation; young children learn far more with a caregiver alongside. Protect meals and the hour before bed as screen-free, and turn off background TV. Your own habits teach more than any rule — and imperfect weeks are normal, so skip the guilt. Are video calls with grandparents really okay for babies? Yes — video chat is the standard exception to the "no screens under two" guidance because it is interactive and social: a responsive face talking to your baby, not content washing over them. It helps to join in and narrate the call for younger babies. We went way over our screen limits this week. Have we done harm? A heavy week — illness, travel, a work crunch — does not define your child’s development. What matters is the typical pattern over months. Simply return to your usual habits without drama, and skip the guilt spiral. What is the best way to end screen time without a meltdown? Give warnings before the end ("one more episode, then we are done"), use natural stopping points like the end of a show rather than mid-scene, and have the next activity ready to start. Consistency helps most — when the rule truly holds every time, children stop negotiating so hard.

title: 2 Month Old Milestones: What Babies Do by 2 Months
description: A clear guide to 2 month old milestones: social smiles, cooing, head control, feeding and sleep patterns, what the checkup covers, and the signs that deserve a call to your baby's clinician.
body: By 2 months, most babies smile when you talk to them, calm down when picked up, coo, react to loud sounds, watch you as you move, look at faces, hold their head up during tummy time, and move both arms and both legs. These skills come from the CDC's revised checklist, which describes what most babies, about 75 percent, can already do by this age. This guide walks through each area, adds a feeding and sleep snapshot, and covers exactly when to call your baby's clinician. What a 2 month milestone checklist really means In 2022, the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics revised their milestone checklists so each item describes what most babies, around 75 percent, can already do by that age. Before the change, many items described the average age, which meant half of all healthy babies had not reached them yet. The new framing makes the list easier to use: if your baby shows a skill, that is reassuring, and if a skill is missing at 2 months, it is a clear signal to mention at the checkup rather than a reason to panic. The checklist ages line up with well visits on purpose, so the 2 month visit is the natural moment to review it. Normal still covers a wide range. Babies work on skills unevenly, so yours might coo constantly but protest tummy time, or follow a slowly moving toy with their eyes while barely smiling yet. If your baby was born early, count from the due date rather than the birth date, so a baby born six weeks early is compared with the 2 week mark, not the 2 month mark. The most useful habit is simple: watch for these skills over a couple of weeks in calm, alert moments, note what you see, and bring the notes to the visit. Comparing your baby with a sibling or another baby the same age tells you very little. Social smiles, cooing, and hearing The social changes are the ones most parents feel first. By 2 months, most babies calm down when spoken to or picked up, look at your face, seem pleased when you come close, and smile when you talk to or smile at them. That first social smile often appears somewhere around 6 to 8 weeks, and it is different from the fleeting smiles of a sleeping newborn: it happens while your baby is awake, looking at you, and responding to you. If your baby has not smiled yet at the visit, say so. Some babies simply need a little longer, and the clinician will want to check hearing and vision as part of the picture. Language at this age means sounds and reactions, not words. Listen for cooing, those soft vowel sounds like ooh and aah, and notice whether your baby reacts to loud sounds by startling, blinking, going quiet, or crying. You can build both skills in ordinary moments. Hold your baby about 8 to 12 inches from your face, talk slowly during feeds and diaper changes, then pause and wait. Many babies will answer with a sound or a wriggle, and that pause teaches the rhythm of conversation. There is no need for special toys or apps. Your voice and your face are the most interesting things your baby has ever encountered. Head control, tracking, and movement On the movement side, most 2 month olds can hold their head up when lying on their tummy, move both arms and both legs, and briefly open their hands. Head control is still wobbly, so keep supporting the head when you lift and carry your baby. During tummy time, expect short lifts of the head rather than a steady push-up, and keep every session supervised while your baby is awake; our newborn tummy time guide covers how to build from there. Pay attention to symmetry too. Babies should use both sides of the body, so mention it at the visit if one arm or leg seems to move much less than the other. Thinking skills at 2 months show up as attention. Most babies this age watch you as you move around the room and can look at a toy or face for several seconds. Vision is still developing, so high contrast helps: bold black and white patterns, a slowly moving rattle, or simply your face drifting from one side to the other. Try moving an object slowly across your baby's field of view and watch the eyes follow it. Brief eye crossing can still be normal this early, but eyes that seem constantly crossed or never track anything are worth mentioning to the clinician. Short, repeated moments of this kind of play do more than long sessions. Feeding and sleep at 2 months Feeding is still frequent at this age. Breastfed babies typically nurse 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, though the pattern often becomes a little more predictable than in the newborn weeks. Formula fed babies usually take larger feeds less often, commonly every 3 to 4 hours. Rather than watching the clock, watch your baby: steady weight gain, plenty of wet diapers, and a baby who seems settled after most feeds are the reassuring signs. Growth spurts can temporarily turn everything upside down, with a day or two of near constant feeding, and then things settle again. If feeding hurts, takes a very long time at every session, or your baby rarely seems satisfied, raise it at the checkup. Most 2 month olds sleep roughly 14 to 17 hours across a full day and night, usually in short, irregular stretches. Some babies begin to give one longer stretch at night around now, and many do not; both patterns are common. Day and night confusion usually eases as you keep days bright and interactive and nights dark, quiet, and boring. Keep following safe sleep basics at every sleep: on the back, on a firm flat surface, in the parents' room but in the baby's own crib or bassinet, with no loose blankets, pillows, or soft toys. A short, repeatable wind down, such as a feed, a fresh diaper, and a song, helps more than any gadget. The 2 month checkup and when to call The 2 month well visit usually includes weight, length, and head measurements, a full physical exam, and a conversation about feeding, sleep, and the milestones above. This is also the visit where the first big round of routine immunizations happens, so plan a quieter day afterward; mild fussiness or a sleepy afternoon is common. Come with questions written down, because they evaporate the moment you are in the room. It helps to note dates, feeding patterns, and anything you have wondered about in the BeMama app or a notebook during the weeks before, then skim your notes in the waiting room. No question about your own baby is too small for this visit. A few signs deserve a conversation sooner rather than later. Talk with your baby's clinician if, by 2 months, your baby does not respond to loud sounds, does not watch things as they move, does not smile at people, does not bring hands toward the mouth, or cannot hold the head up at all when pushing up during tummy time. At any age, losing a skill a baby once had deserves prompt attention. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis, and checklists cannot examine your baby. If something feels off to you, even something you cannot name, say it out loud at the visit. Early questions lead to early answers, and most of those answers are reassuring. Milestone checklists describe what most babies do by 2 months, so a missing skill is a conversation starter, not a verdict. Look for social smiles, cooing, calming when picked up, and clear reactions to loud sounds. Most 2 month olds hold their head up briefly in tummy time and move both arms and both legs. Expect 8 to 12 feeds a day for breastfed babies and roughly 14 to 17 hours of sleep in short stretches. Call the clinician about lost skills, no response to loud sounds, no visual tracking, or no smiles at people. What should a 2 month old be doing? By 2 months, most babies smile at people, coo, calm down when picked up or spoken to, react to loud sounds, watch moving things and faces, hold their head up briefly during tummy time, and move both arms and both legs. These items describe what most babies can do by this age, not a strict deadline. If several are missing, or anything worries you, bring the checklist to your baby's clinician. When do babies start smiling? Most babies give their first social smile somewhere around 6 to 8 weeks, and by 2 months most smile when you talk to or smile at them. Earlier fleeting smiles during sleep are reflexive rather than social. If your baby is not smiling at people by the 2 month visit, mention it; some babies need a little longer, and the clinician can check hearing and vision. How much should a 2 month old sleep? Most 2 month olds sleep roughly 14 to 17 hours in a 24 hour period, usually in short, irregular stretches around the clock. Some begin one longer nighttime stretch around now, and many do not. Keep days bright and nights dark and quiet, and follow safe sleep guidance at every sleep: on the back, on a firm flat surface, with nothing loose in the sleep space. When should I worry about my 2 month old? Contact your baby's clinician if your 2 month old does not respond to loud sounds, does not watch things as they move, does not smile at people, cannot hold the head up during tummy time, or has lost a skill they once had. A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher needs medical attention right away at this age. Feeding refusal, few wet diapers, or unusual floppiness or stiffness also deserve a prompt call. Trust your instincts; asking early is never a mistake.

title: 4 Month Old Milestones: Skills to Expect at 4 Months
description: A calm guide to 4 month old milestones: the social, language, movement, and feeding skills most babies show by four months, plus sleep basics and signs worth a pediatrician visit.
body: By 4 months, most babies smile on their own to get your attention, chuckle, coo back when you talk, hold their head steady without support, bring their hands to their mouth, and push up onto their forearms during tummy time. These skills come from the CDC and AAP milestone checklist, which describes what at least 75 percent of babies can do by this age. Babies vary, and missing one item is rarely a crisis. This guide walks through each area and the few signs that deserve a call to your pediatrician. What most babies do by 4 months Milestone checklists can feel like a test, so it helps to know what they actually measure. The checklist most pediatricians in the United States use, published by the CDC with the American Academy of Pediatrics, lists skills that at least 75 percent of babies show by a given age. In other words, these are things most 4 month olds can already do, not a bar your baby must clear on the exact day they turn four months. Babies work on skills in bursts, and a baby who seems quiet in one area is often busy practicing another. At 4 months the checklist covers four areas. Social skills, like smiling at you on purpose. Language, like cooing and answering your voice with sounds. Cognitive skills, like studying their own hands. And movement, like steady head control and swatting at toys. This guide walks through each area, plus feeding, sleep, and simple ways to play. It also covers the short list of signs that call for a conversation with your pediatrician. If you want the wider month by month picture, that lives in our general baby milestones guide. This page stays focused on month four. Social and language: smiles, chuckles, and coos By 4 months, most babies smile on their own to get your attention, not just in response to your smile. Many chuckle when you play with them, a short giggle rather than a full belly laugh. Bigger laughs usually arrive in the weeks and months that follow, and both patterns are normal. Your baby may also look at you, wiggle, or make sounds to keep your attention once they have it. This is early conversation. The back and forth matters more than the sounds themselves, so pause after you speak and give your baby a turn to answer. Language at this age is cooing: soft, stretched vowel sounds like ooo and aah. Most 4 month olds make sounds back when you talk to them and turn their head toward your voice. You do not need flashcards or special programs to help this along. Narrate what you are doing while you change a diaper or unload groceries, use a warm, musical tone, and copy the sounds your baby makes back to them. Hearing matters here too. If your baby does not seem to respond to your voice or startle at sudden sounds, mention it at the next checkup rather than waiting. Movement: head control, reaching, and tummy time Head control is the headline skill of this age. Most babies hold their head steady without support by around 4 months when you carry them or hold them upright, after months of gradual strengthening. On the floor, most can push up onto their forearms during tummy time and hold a toy when you place it in their hand. You will also see swinging or swatting at dangling toys, and hands finding the mouth again and again. Hands to mouth is not only a hunger sign. It is one of the first ways babies soothe themselves and explore the world. Reaching is clumsy at first, and that is expected. Lay your baby on their back under a play gym, or hold a soft toy just within reach, and let them bat at it. Keep tummy time short and frequent: a few minutes, several times a day, while your baby is awake and you are watching. Some babies also begin rolling around this age. Rolling timelines and the safety changes that come with them are covered in our guide to when babies roll over. Until you have read it, play it safe: never leave your baby alone on a raised surface like a bed or changing table, even for a moment. Feeding and sleep at 4 months Feeding stays simple at this age. Breast milk, formula, or a mix covers everything your baby needs, and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends holding off on solid foods for now. Most babies start solids closer to 6 months, when readiness signs appear, and our starting solids guide covers those signs when you get there. A classic 4 month cognitive milestone shows up at mealtimes: your baby opens their mouth when hungry at the sight of the breast or a bottle. Formula fed babies often take roughly 4 to 6 ounces per feeding every 3 to 5 hours, while breastfed babies nurse on demand, often every 3 to 4 hours during the day. Most 4 month olds sleep about 12 to 16 hours in every 24, counting naps. Night sleep often starts to consolidate into longer stretches, and many babies settle into three or four naps a day, though the exact pattern varies widely from baby to baby. Keep the safe sleep basics steady: on the back, in a bare crib or bassinet, with no loose blankets or pillows. If sleep suddenly falls apart around this age, you may be meeting the well known 4 month sleep regression, which we explain in our sleep regressions guide. A rough sleep patch at 4 months is common and usually temporary. Easy play, and when to call the pediatrician Play at 4 months can be plain and short. Hold your baby in front of a mirror and let them study the face there. Offer one toy at a time for reaching practice. Talk through your day in ordinary words, read a board book, sing the same song at the same point in your routine. At this age repetition is comfort, not boredom, so a familiar game teaches more than a rotating pile of new toys. If it helps you keep track, note new skills, questions, and checkup dates in the BeMama app so they are ready for the 4 month visit. Call your pediatrician if, by around 4 months, your baby does not coo or make sounds back, does not hold their head steady when supported upright, does not bring hands to the mouth, does not watch or swat at toys, or does not smile at people. Also call if your baby loses a skill they once had, at any age. None of these signs is a diagnosis. They are simply the agreed points where a closer look is worthwhile, and support helps most when it starts early. Trust your gut too. You know your baby's ordinary better than any checklist does. Most 4 month olds smile for attention, chuckle, coo back at you, and hold their head steady. Milestone checklists describe what at least 75 percent of babies do by an age, not a pass or fail test. Breast milk or formula covers all nutrition now; most babies start solids closer to 6 months. Expect about 12 to 16 hours of sleep in every 24, naps included, with night sleep starting to consolidate. Call your pediatrician about no cooing, a wobbly head when upright, no hands to mouth, no interest in toys, or any lost skill. What should a 4 month old be doing? Most 4 month olds smile on their own to get attention, chuckle, coo back when you talk, hold their head steady without support, bring hands to their mouth, hold a toy placed in the hand, and push up onto their forearms in tummy time. These come from the CDC checklist of skills at least 75 percent of babies show by this age. A baby can be missing one or two and still be developing typically, so bring questions to the 4 month checkup rather than comparing with other babies. When do babies laugh? Many babies begin to chuckle by around 4 months, and fuller belly laughs often follow over the next month or two. Early laughter usually shows up during play, like gentle bouncing, silly faces, or peekaboo. If your baby smiles and coos but is not laughing yet, that is well within the normal range. Mention it to your pediatrician if your baby is not smiling at people or making sounds back by 4 months. When do babies hold their head up? Most babies hold their head steady without support by around 4 months. Head control builds gradually from birth: brief lifts in the early weeks, a 45 degree lift by around 2 months, and a steady upright head by around 4 months. Regular tummy time while your baby is awake and watched helps build the neck and shoulder strength behind it. If your baby's head still flops or wobbles when held upright at 4 months, bring it up with your pediatrician. How much should a 4 month old eat? A 4 month old still needs only breast milk or formula, with formula fed babies often taking roughly 4 to 6 ounces per feeding every 3 to 5 hours and breastfed babies nursing on demand, often every 3 to 4 hours during the day. Appetite varies from baby to baby and day to day, so watch cues like opening the mouth at the sight of the breast or bottle and turning away when full. Steady weight gain and plenty of wet diapers matter more than exact ounces. Your pediatrician tracks growth at each visit and can confirm your baby is on course.

title: 6 Month Old Milestones: What Babies Do by 6 Months
description: A calm guide to 6 month old milestones: the social, language, movement, feeding, and sleep skills most babies show by half a year, plus signs worth mentioning to your pediatrician.
body: By 6 months, most babies know familiar people, laugh, take turns making sounds, roll from tummy to back, push up on straight arms, reach for toys they want, and explore objects with their mouth. These come from the CDC milestone checklist, which describes skills at least 75 percent of babies show by this age. This guide walks through the half-year snapshot: social, language, movement, feeding, and sleep, plus the signs that are worth a call to your pediatrician. Every baby moves through this list at their own pace, so treat it as a map, not a scorecard. Social and language skills: laughter, squeals, and turn-taking Milestone checklists describe what most babies can do by a given age, not what every baby must do on schedule. The CDC list was revised in 2022 to set each milestone at the age when at least 75 percent of babies show the skill, a deliberate shift from older lists built on 50 percent averages, so a listed skill is one most babies already have. On the social side, the 6-month list includes knowing familiar people, enjoying looking at themselves in a mirror, and laughing. Your baby may light up when you walk in, study your face during feeds, and react differently to a stranger than to a grandparent they see every week. If a few items have not appeared yet, that alone is not a verdict. Babies develop along a range, and the half-year mark is a snapshot, not a test. Language at this age sounds like a conversation without words. Most 6 month olds take turns making sounds with you: you speak, they answer with a coo or a squeal, and back and forth it goes. Blowing raspberries and squealing are normal, and they are useful practice for the mouth muscles that speech will need later. You can help without any special program. Talk through what you are doing, pause so your baby can reply, and copy their sounds back. Narrating a diaper change counts. So does singing badly in the kitchen. The amount of everyday back and forth matters far more than flashcards or apps. Movement: rolling, pushing up, and steadier sitting By 6 months, most babies roll from tummy to back, and many are starting to roll from back to tummy as well. During tummy time, expect your baby to push up on straight arms and hold their chest high off the floor. When you place them sitting, many will lean forward on their hands in a tripod position rather than sitting steadily alone. Independent sitting usually firms up over the following months. We cover the full rolling and sitting timelines in separate guides, so here the point is simply the checklist expectation: rolling at least one direction and pushing up on straight arms are typical by now. Hands are busy at this age. Most 6 month olds reach out to grab a toy they want, bring objects toward their mouth, and explore almost everything by mouthing it. That gumming and licking is not a bad habit. It is how babies gather information about texture, shape, and temperature. Practical safety follows from these new skills. Never leave your baby unattended on a bed, couch, or changing table, because a roll can happen in a second. Keep coins, button batteries, and anything small enough to swallow out of reach, and offer sturdy toys with no loose parts that can break off. Feeding at 6 months: milk still leads, solids begin Around 6 months is when the AAP and WHO point to starting solid foods, alongside breast milk or formula rather than instead of it. Milk remains the main source of nutrition through the rest of the first year, so early solids are about practice, taste, and texture more than calories. Whether your baby is ready depends on skills, not the date on the calendar, and our starting solids guide walks through those readiness signs, first foods, and the puree versus baby-led question in detail, and a separate guide covers introducing allergens like peanut and egg one at a time. A typical day still revolves around milk. Many 6 month olds take a breast or bottle feed every 3 to 4 hours while awake, with one or two small solid sessions tucked in when the baby is rested and mildly hungry rather than starving. Follow your baby's signals instead of a strict clock. Leaning in with an open mouth means more. Closing the lips, turning the head, or pushing food away means done, and by 6 months most babies can tell you this clearly. Respecting those signals now builds a trust in mealtimes that pays off well into the toddler years. Sleep at 6 months: totals and naps Most 6 month olds sleep about 12 to 16 hours in every 24 hours, counting naps, which matches the range pediatric sleep guidance gives for babies between 4 and 12 months. Two to three naps a day is typical at this age, often a morning nap, an early afternoon nap, and sometimes a short late catnap that fades over the coming months. Night stretches are usually longer than they were at 3 months, but plenty of healthy 6 month olds still wake to feed. If night waking is your main question, our guide on sleeping through the night covers that stage in detail. You can support sleep without a complicated system. A short, repeatable wind-down helps: a feed, a fresh diaper, a song or a book, then into the crib drowsy. Keep the room dark and boring during night feeds so they stay brief. Safe sleep still applies at this age: place your baby on their back on a firm, flat surface, in their own crib or bassinet, with no blankets, pillows, bumpers, or soft toys. A baby who rolls both ways can be left in whatever position they settle into, but you should still start every sleep on the back. Play ideas, red flags, and the 6-month checkup Play at 6 months can be simple and repetitive, because repetition is exactly what a learning brain wants. Take turns making sounds and copy your baby's noises back. Play peekaboo with your hands or a light cloth. Offer a baby-safe mirror and watch them study the face inside it. Give washable toys they can mouth freely, and rotate a few favorites rather than piling up many. Daily floor time on a clean blanket gives rolling and reaching room to grow. Reading aloud counts at any age, because your baby is absorbing rhythm and tone long before they understand a single word. Bring your questions to the 6-month checkup, where your pediatrician will measure growth, ask about milestones, feeding, and sleep, and give any vaccines due on the schedule. Call sooner if your baby shows no affection for familiar caregivers, makes no vowel sounds, does not roll in either direction, does not reach for things, seems very stiff or very floppy, or loses skills they once had. None of these is a diagnosis on its own, but each deserves a professional look, and early support helps most when it starts early. It can help to note dates and questions in BeMama or on paper as they occur to you, so the visit covers what matters most. By 6 months most babies know familiar people, laugh, and take turns making sounds with you. Rolling from tummy to back, pushing up on straight arms, and leaning on hands to sit are typical movement skills. Solids usually start around 6 months while breast milk or formula remains the main nutrition. Expect about 12 to 16 hours of total sleep in 24 hours, usually with 2 to 3 naps. Call your pediatrician if your baby is not rolling either direction, not reaching, makes no vowel sounds, shows no affection, or loses skills. What should a 6 month old be doing? By 6 months, most babies know familiar people, laugh, take turns making sounds, blow raspberries, roll from tummy to back, push up on straight arms, reach for toys, and mouth objects to explore them. Many also lean on their hands when placed sitting and close their lips to show they do not want more food. Babies vary, so a missing item is a reason to watch and mention it at the checkup, not a reason to panic. When do babies babble? Many babies start making vowel sounds like ah and eh by around 4 to 6 months, and turn-taking sound games are typical at 6 months. Consonant babbling such as bababa or mamama often follows between about 6 and 9 months. If your baby makes no vowel sounds at all by 6 months, mention it to your pediatrician. How much should a 6 month old sleep? Most 6 month olds sleep about 12 to 16 hours in every 24 hours, including naps. Two to three naps a day is typical, and many healthy babies this age still wake at night to feed. Talk with your pediatrician if your baby consistently sleeps far outside that range or seems exhausted despite normal totals. What happens at the 6 month checkup? At the 6-month checkup, your pediatrician measures weight, length, and head size, asks about milestones, feeding, and sleep, and gives any vaccines due on the schedule. It is a natural moment to raise concerns about rolling, reaching, sounds, or lost skills. Bring your questions written down, because these visits go quickly.

title: 9 Month Old Milestones: Skills to Expect at 9 Months
description: A calm guide to 9 month old milestones: the social, language, thinking, and movement skills most babies show, what the 9 month checkup covers, and when to call your pediatrician.
body: At 9 months, most babies sit without support, respond to their name, string babbling sounds together like mamamama, look for objects that drop out of sight, and rake food toward themselves with their fingers. Stranger shyness, peekaboo giggles, and protest when you leave the room are also right on schedule. This guide walks through each area, plus the nine month checkup, so you know what to expect and what is worth a call to your pediatrician. Social skills: your name, strangers, and peekaboo Around nine months, most babies look when you call their name, even from across the room. Many also become noticeably shy, clingy, or fearful around people they do not know well, including relatives they were happy with a month ago. That shift can feel like a step backward, but it is actually a sign of progress: your baby now clearly knows the difference between familiar people and strangers. You may also notice a protest when you leave the room. That reaction has a name, separation anxiety, and it is a normal part of nine month development rather than a habit you created or a problem you need to fix. Peekaboo usually becomes a favorite around this age. Most babies smile or laugh at peekaboo by nine months because they are starting to understand that a hidden face still exists and will come back. Every round of the game rehearses that lesson, which is one reason it never seems to get old. You can build on it with simple variations: hide a toy under a cloth and let your baby pull it off, or duck behind a door frame and pop out. Keep the pace slow and let your baby take a turn hiding too. These small games are real developmental work dressed up as play, and they cost nothing. Babbling, gestures, and new thinking skills Listen for long strings of repeated sounds: mamamama, babababa, dadadada. At nine months these are usually babble rather than true words, even when they sound convincing, and that is exactly on track. Your baby is practicing the building blocks of speech and learning that sounds get a response. Gestures grow alongside the babble. Many babies now lift their arms to be picked up, a small movement that is really a first conversation: I want something, and I can tell you. Answer both. When your baby babbles, pause, respond, and wait for a reply. This back-and-forth exchange teaches the rhythm of conversation long before real words arrive. Thinking skills take a visible jump around now. Drop a spoon off the high chair tray and your baby will look down to find it, which shows they understand objects still exist out of sight. Expect this game on repeat, because the finding is the fun part. Most nine month olds also bang two things together, shake, and mouth objects to learn what they do. Offer safe household items with different textures and sounds: a wooden spoon and a pot lid work as well as any toy. Narrate what happens in plain words. You are watching cause and effect, memory, and problem solving develop in real time. Movement at nine months, and a word about crawling By nine months, most babies sit without support, and many can get into a sitting position on their own from lying down. Hands are getting busier too. Watch for your baby moving a toy smoothly from one hand to the other and using a raking motion, all fingers sweeping together, to pull small pieces of food toward themselves. The neat thumb-and-finger pincer grasp typically develops between 9 and 12 months, so messy raking is expected right now. Give plenty of supervised floor time on a firm, safe surface. Sitting, reaching, pivoting, and wobbling are all strength training for the bigger movements coming over the next few months. Here is the reassurance many parents need: crawling is not on the CDC's nine month milestone checklist. Many healthy babies are not crawling yet at this age, and some scoot on their bottom, roll everywhere, or skip crawling entirely and move straight toward pulling up and walking. What matters more at nine months is steady sitting, active reaching, and a baby who is clearly working on some way to get around. Crawling ages and styles vary so widely that they deserve their own full guide. If your baby seems floppy or stiff, uses one side of the body much more than the other, or is not sitting with support, bring it up with your pediatrician. Feeding and sleep at nine months A typical nine month old is settling into roughly three meals a day plus breast milk or formula, which remains an important part of nutrition until the first birthday. Finger foods take center stage now that raking and hand-to-mouth skills are working: soft, cooked pieces about the size of your finger that squash easily when pressed. Many families also start practicing sips of water from an open cup or straw cup at meals. Appetite varies day to day, and that is normal. Your job is to offer a range of safe foods on a steady rhythm; your baby's job is to decide how much to eat. Most babies this age sleep somewhere between 12 and 16 hours in every 24, including naps, and two naps a day is the typical pattern at nine months. Do not be surprised if sleep gets bumpy for a stretch. New motor skills, separation awareness, and teething can all disturb nights that were previously settled, and these phases usually pass within a few weeks. A short, predictable bedtime routine helps more than any product: feed, wash, pajamas, a book, a song, into the crib awake if you can. Keep the crib bare, put your baby down on their back, and skip pillows, blankets, and bumpers for now. The nine month checkup and when to call The nine month well visit is more than a weigh-in. It is one of the ages when the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends formal developmental screening, so expect a written questionnaire about how your baby moves, communicates, plays, and solves small problems. Answer it honestly rather than generously; it works best as a snapshot of a typical day. The visit usually also covers growth measurements, a physical exam, feeding and sleep questions, and safety topics like babyproofing for a baby who is about to be mobile. Jot down questions beforehand, and note dates and answers in the BeMama app or a notebook so nothing gets lost between visits. Between visits, trust the pattern more than any single day. Talk with your pediatrician if, by nine months, your baby does not sit even with support, does not babble, does not respond to their own name, does not seem to recognize familiar people, or does not bear weight on their legs when you hold them upright. The clearest reason to call at any age is lost skills: a baby who used to babble or sit and has stopped. None of these signs is a diagnosis. They are simply the agreed points where an early check is worthwhile, and when extra support is needed, starting it sooner helps more. When in doubt, ask; that is what the visit is for. Most 9 month olds sit without support, respond to their name, and babble strings of sounds like mamamama. Stranger shyness, separation protest, and a love of peekaboo are healthy signs of memory and attachment. Crawling is not on the 9 month checklist, and many healthy babies are not crawling yet. The 9 month well visit includes a formal developmental screening questionnaire, so expect detailed questions. Call your pediatrician about not sitting with support, no babbling, no response to their name, or lost skills. What should a 9 month old be doing? Most 9 month olds sit without support, move objects from hand to hand, babble strings of sounds, respond to their name, look for objects that fall out of sight, and smile at games like peekaboo. Babies develop on their own timelines, so one skill arriving a little late rarely means a problem on its own. The pattern across weeks matters more than any single day. Your pediatrician screens all of these areas at the 9 month visit. When do babies respond to their name? Most babies respond to their name by around 9 months, and many begin turning toward it between 6 and 9 months. The response may look like turning, pausing, or glancing up rather than anything dramatic. Try it in a quiet room, since a busy environment makes any baby harder to reach. If your baby does not respond to their name by 9 months, mention it to your pediatrician. Is it normal if my 9 month old is not crawling? Yes. Crawling is not on the CDC's 9 month milestone checklist, and many healthy babies are not crawling at this age. Some scoot, roll, or skip crawling entirely and move straight to pulling up and walking. Talk with your pediatrician if your baby is not sitting with support, seems unusually stiff or floppy, or strongly favors one side of the body. What happens at the 9 month checkup? The 9 month checkup includes growth measurements, a physical exam, and a formal developmental screening questionnaire, since 9 months is one of the American Academy of Pediatrics screening ages. Your pediatrician will ask about feeding, sleep, and safety, and may talk through babyproofing before your baby is fully mobile. Vaccines depend on your baby's record: many babies have none due at 9 months, though a third hepatitis B dose, a seasonal flu vaccine, or catch-up doses may be given. It is a good time to bring your own questions.

title: 12 Month Old Milestones: Your Baby at 1 Year
description: A calm guide to 12 month old milestones: the social, language, cognitive, and movement skills most babies show at 1 year, plus what the 12 month checkup covers.
body: By 12 months, most babies pull to stand, cruise along furniture, wave bye-bye, play games like pat-a-cake, call a parent mama or dada, use a thumb and pointer finger to pick up small foods, and look for things they see you hide. All of those come from the CDC milestone checklist, which describes what 75 percent or more of children do by this age. Walking is not on the 12 month list, so a birthday without first steps is completely normal. Here is what the first year's finish line usually looks like, and what to bring to the 12 month checkup. How to read the checklist at one year The first birthday is a natural moment to step back and ask how your baby is growing. In 2022, the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics revised their milestone checklists so that each item reflects what 75 percent or more of children do by that age. That changes how you should read the list. If your baby does most of the 12 month items, they are keeping pace with the majority of children. If an item is missing, it is a prompt for a conversation with your pediatrician, not a verdict. Babies gain skills in bursts and in different orders, and a child who is busy mastering standing may talk a little later, then catch up quickly. If your baby was born early, count from the due date rather than the birth date when you compare skills with a checklist. Most clinicians adjust for prematurity this way until around age two. It also helps to watch the direction of travel rather than a single snapshot. Jot down new skills with a date, or catch them on video, and look back monthly. A baby who could not pull to stand in October and cruises the couch in December is moving forward, and that trend is what clinicians care about most. And trust your own sense of your child. You watch them more closely than anyone else, and your observations are useful at every checkup. Social and language: games, waves, and first words Social and language milestones at this age look like play. Most 1-year-olds join simple back-and-forth games such as pat-a-cake, and they light up when you take a turn. On the communication side, most wave bye-bye, call a parent mama or dada or another special name, and understand no, which usually shows up as a brief pause or stop when you say it. The word does not need to be crisp. A baby who says mama while reaching for you, or dada when he walks in the door, is using a real word with real meaning, and that counts even when the sounds are still soft around the edges. You do not need flashcards to support any of this. Narrate ordinary moments in short sentences, wave together at every goodbye, and answer babble as if it were conversation, because to your baby it is. Play the games your baby starts, and repeat the ones that make them laugh, since repetition is how they learn the pattern. Keep talking about what they are looking at rather than quizzing them. If you are curious about how words grow from here, and about games that build language over the second year, our guides on language development cover that stage in depth. At 12 months, showing up and taking turns is the whole job. Hands, standing, and getting around Two quiet cognitive milestones are easy to miss. Most 12-month-olds will put something in a container, like a block in a cup, and will look for things they see you hide, such as a toy under a blanket. Both show that your baby now understands objects exist even when they are out of sight. On the movement side, most pull to stand, cruise along furniture while holding on, and drink from an open cup when you hold it steady. Watch the hands too. The pincer grasp, picking up small bits of food between thumb and pointer finger, usually arrives around now and turns every meal into fine motor practice. Notice what is not on the 12 month list: walking. On the revised CDC checklist, taking a few steps alone sits at 15 months, and walking well without holding on to anyone or anything sits at 18 months, so a 1-year-old who cruises but has not let go is right on schedule. Our guide on when babies walk covers the full timeline if you want the detail. To support movement now, clear a safe stretch of floor, let your baby practice barefoot, and place tempting toys on low furniture so cruising has a purpose. Skip the milestone pressure at family gatherings. Babies walk when their balance is ready, and no amount of coaxing at a birthday party moves that date. Eating and sleeping at one year Feeding shifts noticeably around the first birthday. Most 1-year-olds are moving toward soft versions of family foods, cut into small pieces they can pick up themselves. After 12 months, the American Academy of Pediatrics supports switching from formula to plain whole cow's milk, with around two to two and a half cups a day as a common target, and breastfeeding can continue as long as you and your baby want. Keep textures safe: skip whole grapes, whole nuts, hard raw vegetables, and other round or firm foods that can block a small airway. If cups are your current project, our guide on cup and water practice walks through the switch. Sleep needs stay high. Most 1-year-olds do best with about 11 to 14 hours of sleep across 24 hours, counting naps. Many are still on two naps, and some start drifting toward one nap somewhere between 12 and 18 months, often with a messy few weeks in between. Expect some disruption right now even in a good sleeper. New standing skills get practiced in the crib at 2 a.m., and separation feelings often peak around the first birthday, so extra protest at bedtime is common and temporary. A steady, boring routine helps more than any product: same order, same words, same dim room, most nights. The 12 month checkup and when to call sooner The 12 month visit is one of the fuller ones. Your pediatrician will weigh and measure your baby and plot the growth curve, ask screening questions about the milestones above, and talk through feeding, sleep, teeth, and childproofing for a newly mobile child. The visit usually includes several immunizations, and many practices also check for anemia and lead exposure around this age; our vaccination overview covers the schedule itself. Come with questions written down, because they evaporate the moment the appointment starts. Noting new skills, sleep changes, and questions in BeMama or on paper during the weeks before makes the screening questions much easier to answer. A few things are worth raising promptly rather than waiting for the next visit. Tell your pediatrician if your 12-month-old does not stand while holding on to something, does not search for things they see you hide, does not say single words like mama or dada, does not use gestures such as waving, or has lost skills they once had. None of these proves a problem on its own, but each one deserves a closer look, and early support works best when it starts early. If something feels off to you and no checklist captures it, say that too. Asking for a developmental screen is never an overreaction. Most 1-year-olds pull to stand, cruise, wave bye-bye, play pat-a-cake, and say mama or dada. The CDC checklist shows what 75 percent or more of children do, so treat it as a guide, not a race. First steps alone sit at 15 months on the revised checklist, so not walking at the birthday is on schedule. After 12 months, most babies move toward family foods and whole milk and need 11 to 14 hours of sleep. Call your pediatrician about no standing with support, no gestures, no single words, or any lost skills. What should a 12 month old be doing? Most 12-month-olds pull to stand, cruise along furniture, wave bye-bye, play games like pat-a-cake, say mama or dada, understand no, pick up small bits with thumb and pointer finger, and look for objects they see you hide. These items come from the CDC checklist of what 75 percent or more of children do by this age. A baby missing one item is not automatically behind, but it is worth mentioning at the 12 month checkup. When do babies say mama? Most babies say mama or dada with real meaning by around 12 months, and many babble the sounds earlier without attaching them to a person. The word counts when it is aimed at you, such as saying mama while reaching for you. If your baby says no single words at 12 months, mention it to your pediatrician. Is it normal for a 12 month old to not be walking? Yes, not walking at 12 months is normal. The revised CDC checklist places taking a few steps alone at 15 months and walking without holding on at 18 months, so a 1-year-old who pulls to stand and cruises along furniture is on schedule. Do mention it to your pediatrician if your baby is not yet standing with support, or if anything about their strength or movement worries you. What happens at the 12 month checkup? The 12 month checkup usually includes weight, length, and head measurements, developmental screening questions, guidance on feeding and sleep, and several routine immunizations. Many practices also screen for anemia and lead exposure around this age. It is a good moment to raise anything about milestones, milk, naps, or safety, so bring your questions written down.

title: Sleep Regression Ages: 4, 8, 12 and 18 Month Guide
description: A calm guide to sleep regression ages: what happens at 4, 8, 12, and 18 months and 2 years, how long each lasts, and how to respond.
body: Sleep regressions most often happen around 4 months, 8 to 10 months, 12 months, 18 months, and 2 years, and each one typically lasts two to six weeks. A regression is a temporary stretch when a baby who was sleeping better suddenly wakes more at night or fights naps, usually alongside a burst of development. It is a parent term, not a medical diagnosis, and it almost always passes. This guide walks through each age, what drives it, and how to respond without creating new problems. What a sleep regression is and how to spot one A sleep regression is a temporary rough patch, usually two to six weeks, when a baby who had settled into a decent rhythm starts waking more at night, fighting naps, or resisting bedtime. The word regression sounds alarming, but nothing is going backward. These stretches almost always line up with a leap in development: a new motor skill, a language burst, or a change in how your baby experiences separation. Sleep is often the first thing to wobble when the brain is busy. Regression is a term parents and sleep coaches use, not a diagnosis your pediatrician will make, and it does not mean you did anything wrong. The signs of a sleep regression are usually sudden and clustered. A baby who slept long stretches starts waking every hour or two. Naps shrink to twenty minutes or get skipped. Bedtime turns into a protest, and your baby may be clingier or fussier during the day while practicing something new, like rolling or pulling to stand. Appetite and mood are otherwise normal, which is one useful clue that this is development rather than illness. Jot down the date it started somewhere you will find again. Knowing you are two weeks in, not two months, makes the hard nights easier to ride out. The 4 month regression: the one true reset Around 3 to 5 months, babies permanently outgrow newborn sleep. Instead of drifting into deep sleep quickly, they begin cycling through lighter and deeper stages the way older children and adults do, surfacing briefly between cycles. This is a maturation of the brain, not a phase that reverses, which is why the 4 month regression feels different from the others. A baby who used to be fed or rocked into a deep sleep now half-wakes every sleep cycle and notices that the situation has changed: no arms, no bottle, no motion. Each of those surfacings can become a full waking with a call for help. Because the change is lasting, the way through is helping your baby get comfortable with the new sleep pattern rather than waiting for the old sleep to return. Put your baby down drowsy but awake for at least one sleep a day so falling asleep starts to happen in the crib. Keep the room dark, keep a short consistent wind-down, and give it time. Many families ride this stage out with extra support at night and revisit habits later. If wakings stay frequent after several weeks and everyone is exhausted, that is a reasonable moment to read up on gentle settling methods, which our sleep training guide covers in detail. Later regressions: 8 months to 2 years The 8 to 10 month regression usually arrives with big motor skills and big feelings. Babies who are learning to crawl, sit up, or pull to stand often practice in the crib, sometimes getting stuck standing and crying for help. Separation anxiety also tends to ramp up in this window, so being put down and left can suddenly feel like a much bigger deal. Around 12 months, walking, first words, and a growing will can stir sleep again. Some 1 year olds also start refusing the morning nap for a week or two. That protest is usually temporary, and most children genuinely need two naps a while longer. The 18 month regression tends to be driven by independence and language. Toddlers this age are discovering that they have opinions, and bedtime is a natural place to test them. Separation anxiety can flare again, and first molars sometimes overlap, which muddies the picture. Around age 2, sleep can wobble because of nighttime fears, a later bedtime fight, or life changes like a new sibling, toilet learning, or the tempting idea of a big kid bed. Through all of these, the same rule holds: the cause is developmental, the disruption is temporary, and calm consistent responses shorten it. Most toddlers settle back within a few weeks. Regression, teething, illness, or a nap problem? Teething and regressions get blamed for the same nights, but they look different up close. Teething discomfort is usually worst in the few days around a tooth breaking through, and it comes with daytime clues: heavy drooling, gnawing, a tender swollen spot on the gum, and fussiness that eases with comfort. A regression runs longer, comes with new skills or clinginess rather than gum signs, and the daytime mood is often fine. Illness is its own category. Fever, ear pulling or rubbing, a change in feeding, unusual crying, or a baby who simply seems sick warrants a call to your pediatrician rather than a wait and see plan. A mistimed nap schedule can also masquerade as a regression. A baby who is dropping a nap, or being pushed to drop one too early, may fight bedtime, wake overnight, or rise early because daytime sleep pressure no longer matches the schedule. If the disruption built gradually rather than appearing overnight, and there is no new skill or clingy phase to point to, look at the nap schedule first. Our guide to nap transitions walks through the usual ages and how to adjust. Early morning waking has its own set of causes and fixes, and we cover those separately as well. How to respond, and when to call your pediatrician Hold the routine steady. Keep the same bedtime, the same order of steps, and the same sleep space, because familiarity is what your baby anchors to while everything else is changing. Give the new skill plenty of daytime practice so the crib is not the only gym available at 2 a.m. At night, keep checks brief and boring: a low voice, a hand on the chest, minimal light, then out. Comfort freely, but be thoughtful about starting new habits, like a return to feeding to sleep, that you may have to unwind in a few weeks, and skip bed sharing entirely: for babies under 12 months, the safest place to sleep is their own crib or bassinet on a firm, flat surface. It can help to note start dates and wake times in BeMama or a notebook so you can see the pattern instead of guessing. Call your pediatrician if sleep disruption comes with snoring, noisy breathing, or pauses in breathing, with fever, ear pulling, or other signs of illness, or if feeding and weight are a concern. If your baby ever stops breathing, goes limp, or turns blue or gray, that is an emergency: call 911 rather than waiting for an appointment. Also check in if the disruption lasts beyond about six weeks, because at that point something other than a regression may be keeping it going. And if sleep loss is dragging your own mood, safety, or ability to function down, say so at the visit; that matters too. Once a regression has clearly passed but the extra wakings have stuck around as habit, our sleep training guide can help you reset gently. Sleep regressions cluster around 4 months, 8 to 10 months, 12 months, 18 months, and 2 years. Most regressions last about two to six weeks and pass on their own. The 4 month regression is a lasting change in sleep cycles, so help your baby learn to settle rather than waiting it out. Keep the bedtime routine identical, keep night checks brief and boring, and avoid new habits you will have to unwind. Call your pediatrician for snoring, breathing pauses, fever, ear pulling, or disruption lasting beyond six weeks. How long does a sleep regression last? Most sleep regressions last about two to six weeks. The rough patch usually eases once the new skill is mastered or the developmental leap settles. If disrupted sleep drags on past six weeks, look for another cause, such as a nap schedule that needs adjusting or wakings that have become habit, and mention it at your next pediatric visit. What are the signs of a sleep regression? The main signs are a sudden increase in night wakings, shorter or skipped naps, and new resistance at bedtime in a baby who had been sleeping better. Daytime clinginess and intense practice of a new skill, like rolling or standing, often appear at the same time. Appetite and mood are usually otherwise normal, which helps separate a regression from illness. Is it a sleep regression or teething? It is more likely teething if the disruption is brief, peaks in the few days around a tooth coming through, and comes with drooling, gnawing, and a swollen gum. A regression lasts longer, weeks rather than days, and pairs with new skills or separation worries instead of gum signs. Fever or ear pulling points to illness rather than teething, so call your pediatrician if you see either. Is the 4 month sleep regression real, and does it end? Yes, it is real, and the rough patch does end, but the change behind it is permanent. Around 3 to 5 months, babies shift to mature sleep cycles with brief wakings between them, and that pattern is here to stay. Sleep improves once your baby learns to link cycles with less help, which is why practicing settling works better than waiting for old sleep to come back.

title: Nap Transition Ages: 3 to 2, 2 to 1, and Dropping Naps
description: A practical guide to nap transition ages: when babies drop from three naps to two, two to one, and no nap at all, plus readiness signs and schedule tips.
body: Most babies move from three naps to two around 6 to 9 months, from two naps to one between 13 and 18 months, and stop napping entirely between 3 and 5 years. Every one of those ages is a range, and healthy children land all over it. What matters is spotting real readiness, then shifting the schedule gradually enough that your evenings stay survivable. How many naps by age: the quick map Newborns do not follow a nap schedule at all. In the first few months, expect three to five naps of unpredictable length, spread across the day. Somewhere around 4 to 6 months, daytime sleep usually settles into three naps: morning, midday, and a short late-afternoon catnap. Between 6 and 9 months, most babies drop that third nap and run on two. The move to a single midday nap typically happens between 13 and 18 months, and children give up napping altogether somewhere between 3 and 5 years. These are ranges, not deadlines. A healthy child can sit at either edge of every one of them. Total sleep matters more than nap count. Pediatric sleep guidelines recommend 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, naps included, for babies 4 to 12 months, 11 to 14 hours for toddlers aged 1 to 2, and 10 to 13 hours for preschoolers aged 3 to 5. If your child lands inside the range for their age and wakes up reasonably rested, the exact number of naps is a detail, not a problem. Use the totals as your anchor when a transition makes the day feel chaotic. A messy week that still adds up to enough sleep is usually fine. Signs a nap drop is coming, and signs it is not A real nap transition announces itself for one to two straight weeks, not one rough afternoon. The classic signs: your baby fights the last nap of the day almost every day, naps that used to run an hour shrink to 20 or 30 minutes, falling asleep takes far longer than it used to, or a new pattern of early morning waking appears. If you see only a few off days, wait. Teething, travel, illness, and busy developmental stretches can all wreck naps temporarily, and the old schedule usually snaps back within a week or two once life settles. It also helps to rule out a sleep regression before you change anything. Regressions tend to arrive around developmental bursts, hit night sleep as well as naps, and pass within a few weeks with no schedule change at all. True nap-drop readiness builds steadily and does not bounce back. Getting this call wrong has a cost: dropping a nap too early is a common cause of overtired evenings and early waking, and holding on too long can create nap battles. Jot nap start and end times for a week, in the BeMama app or on paper, so you decide from a pattern rather than one bad day. The 3 to 2 nap transition, around 6 to 9 months By 4 to 6 months, many babies settle into three naps: a solid morning nap, a solid midday or early-afternoon nap, and a short catnap late in the afternoon. Between 6 and 9 months, that catnap usually becomes the problem child. Your baby refuses it, or takes it so late that bedtime slides past any reasonable hour. Either version is the signal. The goal of the 3 to 2 transition is simple: two good naps, roughly mid-morning and early afternoon, with a bedtime early enough to absorb the longer stretch of awake time at the end of the day. Work gradually. Stretch the wake time before each of the first two naps by 15 to 30 minutes every few days, so both naps shift later and the third one gets squeezed out of the day. On days the plan collapses and the last stretch turns miserable, move bedtime earlier by 30 to 60 minutes instead of forcing a catnap. An early bedtime is the shock absorber for every nap transition. Most families find this the gentlest drop, with a week or two of mixed days where some days hold three naps and others two. That inconsistency is normal, not a failure. The 2 to 1 nap transition, between 13 and 18 months The move from two naps to one usually happens between 13 and 18 months, and it is often the bumpiest transition of all. Watch for a toddler who plays through the morning nap, or whose morning nap runs so long that the afternoon nap never happens, or who suddenly starts waking very early. Be careful around the first birthday. Many 12-month-olds hit a rough patch tied to walking and other big skills, refuse naps for a week, and then go right back to needing two. Hold the two-nap schedule until the signs have lasted at least one to two weeks. When you are confident, push the morning nap later by 15 to 30 minutes every few days until it lands around midday, then let it stretch long. Serve lunch early during the shift so hunger does not sabotage the nap. On hard days, bring bedtime forward by 45 to 60 minutes, and do not feel guilty about a rescue catnap in the car or stroller. Expect two to four bumpy weeks, with some days on one nap and some on two. Flexibility is the strategy here, not a sign that the transition is going badly. Dropping the last nap, and what replaces it Most children stop napping somewhere between 3 and 5 years, with wide variation at both ends. The signs look familiar by now: lying awake through most of the nap window, a nap that pushes bedtime past a workable hour, or skipped naps that no longer produce evening meltdowns. Some 3-year-olds are genuinely done while some 5-year-olds still need a daily nap, so follow your child rather than the calendar. If daycare requires a rest period, ask whether your child can look at books quietly instead of being expected to sleep. Replace the nap with quiet time rather than dropping midday rest entirely. Keep it at the same time each day: 30 to 45 minutes in a safe room with books and calm toys, no screens. Many children alternate for months, napping some days and resting on others, and an earlier bedtime covers the no-nap days. Mention sleep to your pediatrician if your child snores loudly most nights, seems to gasp or pause in breathing during sleep, or stays exhausted despite plenty of opportunity to rest. Those patterns can point to a sleep problem such as sleep apnea, and they deserve a check, not another schedule tweak. Most babies drop to two naps around 6 to 9 months and to one nap between 13 and 18 months. Wait for one to two weeks of consistent signs before changing the schedule. Stretch wake times by 15 to 30 minutes every few days rather than all at once. Use an earlier bedtime as the buffer on days the new schedule falls apart. Replace the dropped nap with daily quiet time, and expect a few bumpy weeks. When do babies drop to one nap? Most babies drop to one nap between 13 and 18 months. Look for a week or more of fighting one of the two naps, or a morning nap that crowds out the afternoon one. Shift the remaining nap toward midday gradually, and lean on an earlier bedtime while the new schedule settles. What are the signs my baby is ready to drop a nap? The main signs are fighting the same nap for one to two straight weeks, naps that shrink noticeably, long stretches of playing instead of sleeping, or new early morning waking. A few scattered rough days usually point to teething, travel, illness, or a developmental burst rather than readiness. Wait until the pattern is consistent before you change the schedule. When do toddlers stop napping? Most children stop napping between 3 and 5 years old. Common signs include lying awake through the nap window, bedtime drifting very late on nap days, and skipped naps without evening meltdowns. Swap the nap for a daily quiet time of 30 to 45 minutes rather than dropping midday rest all at once. How many naps should my baby take? Newborns take three to five unpredictable naps a day, most babies settle into three naps by 4 to 6 months, two naps around 6 to 9 months, and one nap between 13 and 18 months. Total sleep matters more than nap count, roughly 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours for babies 4 to 12 months, naps included. If your child is generally rested and inside the range for their age, the exact arrangement can vary.

title: Introducing Allergens to Baby: Peanut, Egg and More
description: A calm, practical guide to introducing allergens to baby: when to start peanut and egg, safe first forms, how often to repeat, and which reactions need a call or urgent care.
body: Introduce allergens around 6 months, once your baby has started solids: offer one new allergen at a time in a small, age-safe form, early in the day at home, then keep it in the diet about two to three times a week. Peanut, egg, cow's milk, tree nuts, soy, wheat, fish, shellfish, and sesame are the foods to cover. Most babies handle all of them without a problem, and starting early appears to lower allergy risk rather than raise it. The main exception: if your baby has severe eczema or an existing egg allergy, check in with your pediatrician before starting peanut, since an earlier, supervised start may be recommended. Waiting does not prevent food allergies For years, parents were told to hold off on peanut, egg, and other allergens until well past a baby's first birthday. That advice has been reversed. A large study called LEAP showed that giving peanut early and regularly to high-risk infants lowered their chance of developing a peanut allergy, and guidance from groups like NIAID and the American Academy of Pediatrics changed to match. Delaying allergens does not protect your baby. For many infants, meeting these foods early, while the immune system is still learning, appears to make an allergy less likely, not more. Most babies are ready for allergens around 6 months, once solids are underway and they are managing purees or soft mashed foods without trouble. Do not start solids or allergens before about 4 months. You do not need to master a long list of first foods before adding allergens; a few comfortable feedings are enough of a base. If you are still working out readiness signs and first foods, settle that first, then come back here. Once your baby is eating anything at all from a spoon or their hands, allergens can join the rotation like any other new food. Know the big nine Nine foods cause most food allergies in children: peanut, egg, cow's milk, tree nuts, soy, wheat, fish, shellfish, and sesame. Knowing the list helps you plan, not panic, because most babies tolerate all nine without any drama. Sesame is the one families most often forget, so add it on purpose rather than waiting for it to show up. One clarification about milk: introducing cow's milk protein as an ingredient, like plain yogurt or cheese, is fine in infancy and counts as allergen exposure. Giving cow's milk as a main drink is different and generally waits until around 12 months, because it should not replace breast milk or formula before then. You may see detailed allergen introduction schedules online. A schedule can help you keep track, but there is no required order and no proven perfect sequence. Many families start with peanut and egg because they are among the most common allergens in infancy and the best studied for early introduction, then let the rest arrive through ordinary meals: wheat in infant cereal, soy in mashed tofu, sesame in a thin smear of tahini, fish well cooked and flaked, yogurt stirred into fruit. Tree nuts and shellfish can follow in the same spirit, in age-safe textures, one new food at a time. One at a time, early in the day, at home Offer a new allergen at home, early in the day, when your baby is healthy and in a decent mood. Mornings are practical because you have the rest of the day to watch, and your pediatrician's office is open if a question comes up. Start small: about a quarter teaspoon of the allergen mixed into a food your baby already accepts. If that goes down without a problem, offer a little more the next time. Introduce only one new allergen on a given day. If two new foods arrive together and a rash appears, you will not know which one caused it. After the first taste, keep an eye on your baby for the next couple of hours, since most reactions show up within minutes to about two hours. Once a food is tolerated, the job is not done: keep it in the diet, about two to three times a week, because regular exposure is what seems to maintain tolerance. It helps to note the date, the food, and anything you noticed in BeMama or a notebook, so the pattern is easy to review later. Skip home shortcuts like rubbing food on your baby's skin; skin contact can cause harmless redness and tells you little about true allergy. Safe forms for peanut, egg, and the rest Whole nuts and thick globs of nut butter are choking hazards and stay off the menu; whole nuts should wait until around age 4 or later. For peanut, thin smooth peanut butter with warm water, breast milk, or formula until it is drizzly, or stir it into a fruit or vegetable puree. Peanut powder or peanut flour mixed into oatmeal or yogurt works just as well. For egg, serve it well cooked: scrambled soft, or hard boiled and mashed with a little water or puree. Skip runny, raw, or lightly cooked egg for babies. The same principle runs across the list: familiar texture, allergen inside. Some babies should see the pediatrician before starting peanut. If your baby has severe eczema, an existing egg allergy, or both, the chance of peanut allergy is higher, and current guidance supports introducing peanut earlier, often around 4 to 6 months, with a clinician involved. That visit might include allergy testing, a first supervised taste in the office, or simply a green light with instructions. Mild eczema does not usually need this step, but when you are unsure, ask. A short conversation at a regular checkup is enough to sort out which path fits your baby. What a reaction looks like, and what to do Most reactions are mild and appear within minutes to about two hours: a few hives near the mouth or on the face, new redness, mild swelling, vomiting, or unusual fussiness. If you see this, stop offering the food, wipe your baby's face and hands, and call your pediatrician before serving that food again. Take a photo of any rash while it is visible, since hives often fade before an appointment. Plain redness around the mouth can also come from acidic foods like tomato or citrus irritating the skin, and your clinician can help you tell the difference. A small set of signs means call 911 or your local emergency number right away: widespread hives, swelling of the lips or tongue, trouble breathing, wheezing or persistent coughing, repetitive vomiting, sudden paleness, or a baby who becomes limp, floppy, or unusually sleepy. Do not wait to see whether it passes, and do not drive a struggling baby yourself if emergency help can come to you. Severe reactions are uncommon, but they move fast, and treatment works best early. If a food allergy is confirmed later, your clinician will help you build a full action plan for home and daycare. Delaying allergens does not prevent food allergies, and early peanut introduction can lower risk. Introduce one new allergen at a time, early in the day, at home, starting with about a quarter teaspoon. Once a food is tolerated, keep it in the diet about two to three times a week. Use safe forms: thinned peanut butter or peanut powder and well-cooked egg, never whole nuts. A few hives near the mouth means stop and call your pediatrician; breathing trouble, swelling, or floppiness means call 911. When should I introduce peanut butter to my baby? Around 6 months for most babies, once solids have started, and not before about 4 months. Thin smooth peanut butter with water, breast milk, or formula, or stir it into a puree, because thick spoonfuls are a choking hazard. If your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy, talk with your pediatrician first, since earlier, supervised introduction may be recommended. How do I give my baby egg for the first time? Offer well-cooked egg, such as soft scrambled egg or hard boiled egg mashed into a familiar puree, starting with about a quarter teaspoon. Serve it early in the day at home and watch your baby for a couple of hours afterward. Avoid runny, raw, or lightly cooked egg for babies. If it goes well, keep egg in the diet about two to three times a week. What are the signs of an allergic reaction to food in a baby? The most common signs are hives, redness, swelling, vomiting, or unusual fussiness within minutes to about two hours of eating. A few hives near the mouth means stop the food and call your pediatrician. Widespread hives, lip or tongue swelling, trouble breathing, repetitive vomiting, or a limp, floppy baby are emergency signs: call 911 right away. What are the top 9 allergens for babies? The big nine allergens are peanut, egg, cow's milk, tree nuts, soy, wheat, fish, shellfish, and sesame. Together they account for most food allergies in children. There is no required order for introducing them, though peanut and egg are the best studied for early introduction, and each should arrive one at a time in an age-safe form.

title: Baby Finger Foods: What to Offer by Age and Choking Safety
description: A practical guide to baby finger foods: when to start, how to cut each food safely by age, which choking hazards to avoid, and how to tell gagging from choking.
body: Most babies are ready for soft finger foods around 8 to 9 months, once they can sit steadily, pick up pieces of food, and mash them with their gums. Teeth are not required. What matters most is texture and size: every piece should squish between two of your fingers and be cut so it cannot block a small airway. This guide walks through what to offer at each stage and which foods to avoid until around age 4. When babies are ready for finger foods Look for three skills before offering finger foods. Your baby sits steadily with little or no support, reaches for food and brings it to their mouth, and makes chewing motions, even without a single tooth. Gums are surprisingly good at mashing soft food, so teeth are not a requirement. Most babies show these skills around 8 to 9 months, usually after a few weeks of practice with mashed or lumpy solids. If your baby has only just started solids, our starting solids guide covers those first weeks; this article picks up once your baby wants to feed themselves. Every baby moves at their own pace. Some grab at food eagerly from the first weeks of solids, while others need until closer to 10 months to manage soft pieces. Watch skills rather than the calendar, and if your baby was born early, count from the due date rather than the birth date. Around 9 months, many babies develop a pincer grasp, picking small pieces up between thumb and finger, and that skill changes what you can safely offer. If your baby shows little interest in self feeding by around 9 to 10 months, or consistently struggles with lumps, mention it at the next checkup rather than worrying alone. The squish test: getting texture and size right Use a simple test before anything goes on the tray: the piece should squish easily between your thumb and finger, the way ripe banana or a well-cooked carrot does. If it does not squish, cook it longer, grate it, or save it for later. For a baby who still grabs with the whole fist, cut food into strips about the size of your little finger. Your baby holds the strip and gnaws on the part sticking out of their hand, which builds chewing skills while the shape keeps the food easy to control. Slippery foods like avocado are easier to hold with a light dusting of infant cereal. Once the pincer grasp appears, usually around 9 months, shift to pieces about the size of a pea. Shape matters as much as size. Round foods can block a small airway, so cut grapes, cherry tomatoes, and similar foods into quarters lengthwise, never into coins. Slice sausages and hot dogs lengthwise first, then chop them small. Cook hard fruits and vegetables such as apple and carrot until soft, or grate them raw. Remove skins that could peel off in sheets, along with pits, seeds, bones, and tough crusts. When in doubt, make the piece softer and smaller than you think you need. What to offer at each stage From around 8 to 9 months, good first finger foods include soft cooked vegetable pieces such as sweet potato, carrot, and zucchini, strips of ripe banana, avocado, or very ripe peeled pear, well-cooked pasta, lightly toasted bread strips, and strips of omelet or scrambled egg. Shredded cheese and small pieces of soft flaked fish with all bones removed work well too. None of these need teeth. If common allergy foods such as peanut or egg are still new to your baby, our guide on introducing allergens covers how to offer them. Keep portions tiny; a few pieces at a time helps prevent cheek stuffing. From 9 to 12 months, the pincer grasp lets you offer pea-sized pieces of soft cooked chicken or other tender meat, well-cooked beans lightly squashed, small pasta shapes, chopped soft fruit, grated raw apple or carrot, and pieces of pancake or soft flatbread. After the first birthday, most babies can eat small, soft pieces of whatever the family eats, lightly seasoned and cut with the same care. The choking rules do not relax just because your child has a few teeth, since the molars that do real grinding arrive much later. Keep offering variety and let your baby set the pace at each meal. Choking hazards to avoid before age 4 Some foods are risky because they are small, round, firm, slippery, or sticky, which is exactly the combination that can lodge in a young child's airway. The main foods to avoid or modify until around age 4 include whole grapes and cherry tomatoes, hot dog or sausage coins, whole nuts and seeds, popcorn, hard candy, marshmallows, gum, chunks of raw hard vegetables or apple, large chunks of meat or cheese, and thick spoonfuls of nut butter. These foods appear on pediatric choking lists again and again because their size and texture match a young airway. The risk does not depend on how careful or capable your child seems. Many of these foods are fine with a simple change. Quarter grapes and cherry tomatoes lengthwise so no piece stays round, and do the same with large firm blueberries. Slice hot dogs lengthwise into thin sticks before chopping. Spread nut butter in a thin layer on toast or stir it into yogurt or warm cereal instead of offering it from a spoon. Cook carrots, apples, and other hard produce until soft, or grate them finely. Finely ground nuts can be mixed into food. Popcorn, whole nuts, hard candy, and gum have no safe modification at this age, so save them for later childhood. Gagging, choking, and safe mealtime habits Gagging is loud; choking is quiet.
